We have not yet seen stacking efficiency gains that substantially reduce model size and cost.

7:18 The labs haven't even hardened their own infrastructure
The author thinks the biggest short-term risk may be that AI labs don't take safety seriously enough — they haven't hardened their own infrastructure, letting AI misuse spread. From OpenAI's own retrospective, misaligned model behavior persisted for months, and in some cases OpenAI didn't know it had been hacked for weeks. Response times are too long, and this is not unique to OpenAI. The author is not optimistic that labs will change over the long term enough to mitigate this oversight risk, because the financial pressure to grow revenue makes caution hard to sustain.

7:18 Open model supporters are now the most exposed
The author says he is especially exposed in the current environment as an open model supporter. If an open model were used by a third-party organization to deliberately hack another company — like the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident but intentional — he expects the result to be severe restrictions on stronger open models. But open models are necessary for many organizations doing cybersecurity hardening, and for adapting to new AI risks in the future. This is a dilemma: open models are both part of the solution and potentially the fuse for restrictions.

7:18 Agent clusters are not new independent entities
The author's repeated reading of the emerging agent clusters is: they are trying to complete the tasks given to them, bypassing expected paths using skills we didn't know they had. This is a huge victory — squint and AI is doing what we told it to do. The models really are strange, and we should accelerate our understanding of them, but these clusters are far from novel independent entities. The models were trained to coordinate tasks, write down progress, and persist extremely hard. Codifying our current uncertainty about how AI works into a certainty that we will not understand AI in the future is a kind of giving up.

item.title: You Can't Build Superintelligence Inside a Data Centre: The Bottleneck Is Real-World Signal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-eightythousand-数据中心里造不出超级智能-瓶颈是真实世界的信号/
item.description: Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.
item.content:encoded:
Automating AI R&D is not the same as superintelligence: Tom Reed argues that for most tasks the data only exists once you deploy models in real markets, and neither sample efficiency nor simulation can fill the gap — the singularity is stuck on signal, not compute.

Tom Reed pushes the argument that ‘signal is sovereign’ all the way to the end, and it will change how you judge AGI timelines and AI lab strategy; the analogies are sharp and the density is high.

2:54 The bottleneck for the singularity is signal, not compute
Tom's positive claim is not that superintelligence is impossible, but that it cannot be stacked up inside a data centre. His mechanism: to be good at solving problems, you need a source of problems, and that source can only be hard interaction with the real world in serial time. He compresses this into one line — ‘signal is sovereign’ — bodies need pain, companies need profit, models need real deployment. So he judges that the arrival of superintelligence depends on deploying AI into the economy expensively, painfully and slowly, not on how much more compute gets piled up inside a lab.

5:01 Jaggedness won't disappear before the singularity
The current way capabilities advance does not support the claim that ‘the model is accumulating a general g’: models only get better at the things they have a chance to practise, so the capability boundary is more uneven than anyone expected. In 2016 nobody would have predicted a model that beats Stanford Law graduates on the bar exam yet can't play tic-tac-toe reliably. Tom thinks jaggedness is mainly a product of the training data distribution, and there is no reason to believe automating AI R&D would end it, so he proposes Toner's Law: we should expect jaggedness to persist longer than expected, even after we have adjusted for it.

6:01 Patchwork RL won't buy you general intelligence
Tom zeroes in on the current toolbox for capability progress: custom RL environments are the main engine. In Mechanize's telling, each environment is a single engineer spending a week patching one specific failure observed on a real frontier model; in Zhengdong Wang's telling, scaling used to hand you a bundle of capabilities at once, and now they have to be unlocked one by one with effort. Tom's challenge: are we really going to do the singularity one problem per week? If RL genuinely generalised, AI companies should already have the evidence; when Dwarkesh kept pressing Dario, every one of Dario's rebuttals was just a weak analogy between RL and the pretraining generalisation of the GPT-2 era.

8:26 For most tasks the relevant data is zero
The common rebuttal is that LLMs are wildly sample-inefficient and could improve enormously, and AI bulls point smugly at DeepSeek reaching GPT-4 level on a fraction of the compute. Tom doesn't buy it: Anson Ho and Beren Millidge both point out that gains in intelligence per FLOP come mainly from data quality rather than algorithm quality, and pure algorithmic innovation yields fairly weak returns at constant compute. More fundamentally, for most tasks the relevant data simply doesn't exist — improving sample efficiency by orders of magnitude still multiplies zero. His test: if the internet had never existed, how much progress could today's talent and compute make on writing code? His guess is tens of billions of human-hours.

11:40 Text about a task is not the task
For most economically interesting tasks, what's in the corpus is description, commentary or advice, not a record of performing the task itself. Dominion is a board game with a huge body of strategy writing, yet Claude plays it badly: the training process that teaches it to write beautiful articles about Dominion is a different thing from building an agent that can win, because the optimisation target is ‘the advice looks good’ rather than ‘the strategy wins’. Tom's analogy is that the LLM's relationship to most tasks is a bit like McKinsey's relationship to running a company. The exception is writing code — the tokens are themselves constitutive of the task — which is why training AlphaZero on chess commentary rather than games is the anomaly.

14:06 The score went up, the real capability didn't
How does self-improvement inside a data centre know it has actually got stronger? Of the submissions on SWE-bench accepted by AI automated graders, close to half are rejected by the real human maintainers of the relevant codebase — the score can be pumped up while the merge rate doesn't move. Tom asks in return: how is Claude 8 supposed to tell, from the results of a Become-POTUS eval alone, whether its brilliant new algorithm actually improved Claude 9's ability to become president? Evals are useful, but they are always stubbornly incomplete proxies; the only eval that ultimately counts is voters, customers, the economy and the P&L. Without those, your singularity gets ruthlessly Goodharted.

15:28 Market data isn't hidden, it doesn't exist yet
The second layer of doubt is more fundamental and more speculative: even an arbitrarily intelligent simulator cannot generate practice data for many tasks, because that data can only be produced through interaction with the relevant market. This is Hayekian: that something is good is a signal generated by millions of actors revealing preferences through behaviour, and it cannot be simulated inside a data centre — it's not that data collection happens to fail, it's that the data doesn't exist anywhere yet. He uses his own board gaming as the analogy: a game of Twilight Imperium takes 12 hours, he'll plan weeks ahead until he feels certain of winning, and about 5 minutes into the real game his predictive power goes to zero. Continual learning doesn't save you either, because without a genuinely diverse problem set you can't tell which algorithm is better.

21:17 The winner may be the deployer itself
Corollary one: a policy focus on ‘internal deployment’ and ‘automating AI R&D’ may be misplaced — superintelligence isn't impossible, it just won't arrive in the shape currently imagined, on the timeline currently predicted; the next phase looks more like the grind of deployment, customer discovery and real data collection. Corollary two: data holders have far more power than they realise (Ukraine is one example), and the asymmetry between ‘companies that can build frontier models’ and ‘entities holding proprietary deployment data from real economic activity’ could flip. Corollary three: labs may conquer vertical industries one at a time, and the way to win is to become the deployer yourself.

item.description: Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.
item.content:encoded:
Coinbase wants every AI agent to have its own account: 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents, and the minimum credit card fee is exactly 30 cents — the old payment rails can't carry the machine economy.

The part about how Coinbase uses AI internally is the most valuable: one "brain" per service, corrections must be written back, and the mechanism is concrete enough to copy; agent payments come with hard numbers, while the new drug section is more opinion than detail.

6:47 76% of machine payments are under 30 cents
Armstrong says agents are already generating a flood of transactions worth a few cents: VC firms scraping paywalled data for research, recruiters crawling LinkedIn, one agent calling another specialised agent as a tool to fetch source data. But the minimum per-transaction fee on a debit or credit card is a flat 30 cents plus a percentage, so the old rails basically don't work below $1 — paying 30 cents to move 1 cent makes no sense. The number he gives: about 76% of the agentic commerce transactions they see are under 30 cents. That is the hardest argument for stablecoins and crypto rails cutting into the machine economy.

11:42 Build a "brain" for every service
Coinbase has built a "brain" for every team, every repo, every service and even every employee: it holds every incident that service has ever had, the financial controls that must be enforced, every A/B test that has been run, the full GitHub history, and which PRs were accepted or rejected. When an agent comes to change code, it reads this brain first. The truly critical step: when a human reviewer finds the agent missed something, they are not allowed to just hand-edit and merge — that correction must be written back into the brain. That way one correction covers all future scenarios, and the one-shot PR rate keeps climbing, something Armstrong calls "recursive self-improvement".

15:00 The CEO runs 10 agents on code at once
Armstrong says that now, when he hits an idea or a bug, he no longer pings the team all day — he drops the comment into an internal harness (they call it Toshi) and sends over a finished PR for review, which he says is addictive. He has also pushed the CEO back into writing features: have an expensive frontier model break a complex feature into three phases of ten things each, then have it recommend which cheaper model each subtask should use, then run 10 agents in parallel on phase one. He says that over the course of recording this podcast, all 10 items got done and were waiting for his review.

17:02 What gets killed is tasks, not people
On whether AI will make companies smaller, Armstrong's judgment is: productivity really is rising, but that is a separate matter — what gets automated or eliminated is tasks, not people. He does not think a company like Coinbase shrinks to 10 people; rather, the people already there can do vastly more and everything speeds up; and two-person and five-person companies will indeed produce volumes that used to be unimaginable. The result is that the cost curve of revenue relative to headcount changes: the same group of people produces far more, and margins should rise over the long run. He does not close the door on it — some companies will still hire at the same pace.

18:33 88% of revenue no longer comes from Bitcoin trading
Armstrong cites the numbers from the earnings report: 88% of revenue now comes from non-Bitcoin trading. The interesting part is that Coinbase's stock price is still highly correlated with the Bitcoin price. He says he loves Bitcoin, sees it as digital gold and sound money for everyone in the world, but crypto is updating every part of the financial system. The tokenised equity product he just announced is currently only available outside the US, and they are talking to regulators about a US path; he stresses that these are real equities — backed 1:1 by real securities held in custody, not synthetics, derivatives or debt instruments.

21:57 Prediction markets are more than sports betting
Armstrong says prediction markets are growing extremely fast inside the Coinbase app: within a few months of launch they reached roughly $100 million in annualised revenue, growing more than 100% quarter over quarter. Sports is indeed part of it, and he sees that as a form of entertainment worth celebrating — but he thinks it is much bigger than that, and that the societal implications are not yet fully understood. His example is policy: to judge whether a policy should be implemented, you could first form a prediction market on "what will the unemployment rate be one, two, three years after implementation". Further out are big questions with no clear settlement date, like "is there a God", which he calls opinion markets, with a mechanism like buying a stock — you are just betting on whether it gets better or worse.

31:53 Restore cells to their youthful function
New Limit takes the epigenetic reprogramming route: it does not change the cell type (the Yamanaka-lab style approach does), it only restores the cell's youthful function. The platform first uses AI to search the vast combinatorial space of transcription factors for candidates, runs large-scale pooled screens, then functional experiments (mostly animal models), and finally human trials. The first batch targets three cell types: hepatocytes, vascular cells and T cells of the immune system. The first Phase 1 trial is in alcoholic liver disease (ALD), where patients have almost no option besides a liver transplant and survival after diagnosis at 12 months is very low. Armstrong estimates this one drug alone could be worth $20 billion if it succeeds, but the goal is for a 40-year-old to have the liver, immune system and blood vessels of a 20-year-old.

41:10 What America lacks is not land, it's sandboxes
Armstrong's interest in special economic zones comes from a "meta-question": what is slowing down progress — in many places, it is over-regulation. He mentions that Coinbase invested in Prospera in Honduras, and thinks they have had ups and downs with the local government but are close to resolving it. During the campaign there was discussion of an idea called "freedom cities": the federal government holds vast tracts of land, take 10 or 100 square miles, and on that land you don't have to go through the usual EPA process — you can build data centres, nuclear power plants, unlimited drone delivery without getting FAA approval item by item — first test what works in a safe, controlled sandbox, and once it works, push it back out to the whole country through the normal process. He says the problem now is that in many cases there is simply no sandbox to test in, and if entrepreneurs can't iterate they can't solve the problem.

item.title: Take a Spending Test Before You Marry: Tightwads and Spendthrifts Attract Each Other, and Divorce More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-rationalreminder-结婚前先做花钱测试-紧手和挥霍者互相吸引-也更容易离婚/
item.description: Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes are more likely to attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.
item.content:encoded:
Research sorts spenders into tightwads and spendthrifts. The two extremes are more likely to attract each other, but after marriage they have more money conflicts and lower marital satisfaction; and the more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk.

Medium information density. The first half is spending-personality research; the second half — on prenups, wedding spending and who holds financial decision power in a household — is more valuable. Skim-friendly.

7:05 A tightwad isn't frugal — spending physically hurts
Scott Rick and coauthors proposed in 2008 a spending scale running from tightwad to spendthrift. The core isn't how much you spend but ‘anticipatory pain’ — the emotional reaction you feel at the moment of paying. Tightwads feel too much pain from spending and spend less than they ideally would; spendthrifts feel too little and spend more than they ideally would. The scale measures the gap between your ‘ideal self’ and your actual behavior, so a very rich person can be a tightwad and someone near bankruptcy can be a spendthrift. On the show, Ben retook the test and scored 11, just over the tightwad line; Dan scored 16, an unconflicted consumer.

22:15 Tightwads and spendthrifts are precisely the ones who attract each other
Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than another tightwad. The authors' explanation: people have poor introspective ability about what will attract them in a real partner; when someone else displays the same flaw you have, it reminds you of that negative trait. Hence ‘fatal fiscal attractions’ — the other person lacks your spending vice, so at first they seem especially attractive. But the excitement is temporary. Afterward, tightwad-spendthrift couples have more frequent money conflicts and lower marital happiness; the larger the gap on the scale, the more pronounced the conflict, even controlling for household debt and savings.

28:17 Everyone already has a default prenup
In Ontario it's called a marriage contract; elsewhere, a prenup. The key premise: when you marry, you already have a default agreement under your jurisdiction's family law, so the first step is to find out what the default terms are, then decide whether to write your own. Not marrying can also have legal consequences — cohabiting, or having children without marrying, can still produce legal effects on separation. Why so few use one? First, optimism bias: engaged couples can accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimate their own divorce probability far lower, so the agreement they sign doesn't seriously consider the scenario it's meant to govern. Second, signaling cost: proposing a prenup is itself treated as a negative signal of ‘lack of commitment to the relationship’, making the other party less willing to raise it.

40:23 The more a wedding costs, the higher the divorce risk
A 2021 paper in the Journal of Consumer Policy surveyed more than 3,000 married people and, after controlling for income, demographics and relationship factors, found the opposite of intuition: the more a man spent on an engagement ring, the higher the divorce risk; the more a woman spent on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress may be one mechanism. Couples with the lowest divorce rates spent less than $1,000 on their wedding. But the same study found two kinds of wedding spending that predicted longer marriages: more guests, and going on a honeymoon — neither related to price. Ben's wedding cost about $300, with only his sister, parents and wife present; Dan's cost about $5,000 for 150 people, saving money with a free photographer, a friend making the cake and gifts.

46:29 The benefits of merging finances may come from ‘thinking’, not ‘doing’
A 2022 meta-analysis covering six studies and more than 38,000 people found that couples who fully merge finances have higher relationship satisfaction and are less likely to break up, and this holds across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found joint accounts promote communal norms, shared goals and good feelings about ‘team money management’. But more counterintuitive is a 2025 paper by Johan Yana Pet: directing people's attention to an existing joint account rather than their separate accounts produces similar effects — that is, thinking of finances as ‘ours’ rather than ‘yours and mine’ itself makes people talk about money more and more effectively, regardless of how accounts are actually set up. Another 2022 paper found that increases in jointly held wealth raise life satisfaction, while increases in individually held wealth have no significant effect.

53:32 Financial infidelity is a deeper problem than spending disagreements
Financial infidelity is defined as: engaging in financial behavior you expect your partner would disapprove of, then hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more prone to financial infidelity than the other, couples are more likely to move toward separate financial goals rather than shared ones, and it predicts lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction; this holds even after controlling for mismatches like tightwad/spendthrift. Joint accounts increase transparency, but if someone deliberately conceals, even a joint account can be supplemented with a hidden one, and the problem escalates from money to trust. Dan's judgment: if someone is committing financial infidelity, switching to a joint account either forces them to find another way or puts the problem on the table and leads to separation — which is beyond the scope of financial planning.

57:36 In household asset allocation, the husband's preferences are systematically amplified
A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper found that Australian households, at the household level, incorporate on average 60% of the husband's risk tolerance and only 40% of the wife's, which the authors say implies a 20-percentage-point bargaining gap; half comes from observable characteristics like income and employment, the other half attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining power is 69% in Germany and 61% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable but all exceed 60%. A 2021 Journal of Finance paper found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal financial literacy, which the authors say is best explained by gender identity norms rather than ability differences; the mechanism indicated by randomized experiments: female identity suppresses a wife's willingness to voice ideas, while male identity makes a husband less responsive to his spouse's input.

1:00:41 Overtrading costs men nearly a percentage point a year
Barber and Odean's 2001 study of 35,000 brokerage accounts found men trade 45% more frequently than women, consistent with the prediction that overconfidence leads to harmful overtrading. Trading has costs: overtrading reduces men's net returns by 2.65 percentage points a year and women's by 1.72. Both groups hurt themselves by trading too much; women just do less of it. Dan adds that among the client couples he sees, the primary contact is almost evenly split between men and women; but when the man is the primary contact, conversations are more about the portfolio, and when the woman is, more about planning. He also observes some male clients asking questions they ‘feel they should ask’, more like performance, while female clients almost never do this.

item.title: Insects Are Disappearing, but Pesticides Aren't the Biggest Killer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-sciencevs-昆虫正在消失-但杀虫剂不是最大凶手/
item.description: Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.
item.content:encoded:
Insect declines keep getting dismissed as exaggerated, but global data still points the same way; the real underrated culprit isn't agriculture, it's the pesticides ordinary people buy and spray themselves.

Medium information density; the first half leans into dragonfly genitalia for shock value, but the parts on pesticide regulatory blind spots and the successful eradication of the giant hornet are worth hearing.

8:55 The 70% decline was challenged, but the data keeps piling up
A decade ago, a European study covering 30 years of data showed insect total mass in one place had fallen 70%. Jessica herself raised doubts at the time: you can't directly compare heavy beetles with light mosquitoes, maybe it's just a shift in composition. But since then scientists have sampled repeatedly around the world, north to south, from the roots of the insect evolutionary tree to its top, and they keep seeing the same pattern — a rate of decline never seen before. She concedes some pest cockroaches and some bee species are doing better, but the insects in the other column that are declining are ‘still astonishingly high in number, and increasing.’

19:02 Pesticides aren't an agriculture problem, they're a your-backyard problem
The host assumed the answer would be agricultural chemicals, but Jessica turned the spotlight on ordinary people. Agricultural pesticide use is tightly regulated, with rules on how much and what kind, and farmers don't want to spend more than they have to. But ‘you and I’ can go buy any pesticide tonight and spray it wherever we want, with no regulation at all. She mentions the host ordering a pesticide from the US that is banned in Australia, and her response is ‘wear gloves and a mask.’ She calls the overall picture what her colleague David Wagner calls ‘death by a thousand cuts’ — drought, floods, fire, nitrogen deposition, land-use change, noise, light pollution, chemical pollution, invasive species, with no single cure.

22:24 Colony collapse was only ever the story of domesticated honeybees
The colony collapse disorder that caused panic a decade ago was actually only about Apis mellifera, the European domesticated honeybee, not a North American native species. They get trucked around the country in huge trailers, live under heavy stress, and on top of that face Varroa mites and neonicotinoid pesticide residues. Jessica's criticism: worrying only about this one domesticated, managed bee is like not worrying about any mammal going extinct except the cow we like to eat. What's actually needed is holistic bee health, which is also why pollinator gardens have become popular — plant native species for all the pollinators in the environment.

24:13 America's biggest irrigated crop is lawn
NASA researchers estimated in 2005 that the US has more than 30 million acres of lawn, including golf courses, and by surface area lawn is the single largest irrigated crop in the country. Jessica's advice is concrete: shrink the lawn, keep the part you play on, don't mow the edges, let it go wild; or just plant a pollinator garden. She did exactly that on the slope in front of her house, and got ‘garden shamed’ by neighbors on the community social media, because a pollinator garden needs native plants of different heights and bloom times, and looks ugly for the first few years.

27:16 Spotted lanternfly honeydew invites mold
The spotted lanternfly is a Hemiptera, its mouthparts a suction pump plus a straw that stabs into plants to drink sap; an all-liquid diet means its excrement is basically sugar water, known as honeydew. This sticky honeydew rains down on the environment, and certain molds and fungi grow on it, potentially harming plants. They have more than 70 host plants, their preferred host being the equally invasive tree of heaven, but they can also take maples, apples, and unfortunately grapes. As they spread west toward California's big grape-growing regions, that's the real worry.

30:28 The giant northern hornet was completely eradicated
The so-called murder hornet is now renamed the giant northern hornet, and Jessica finds the old name a bit stigmatizing. She calls this story a success case of human collaboration: a homeowner saw an unfamiliar insect on their tree, didn't ignore it, and reported it; the specimen reached a colleague at the Smithsonian and was identified; the government put up money, people on the West Coast mobilized immediately, found the location and cleared it. A piece of wood from that tree is still on display at the Smithsonian, because it holds a batch of individuals. In December 2024, the USDA announced the hornet had been eradicated.

33:46 Cockroach milk is secreted by modified spiracles
Most cockroaches lay egg cases called oothika, which look like little coffee beans; when they hatch, all the larvae take a breath at once and pop the ‘little box’ open. But cockroaches like diploptera punctata are ovoviviparous, and the mother feeds the embryos a milk-like secretion. Insects aren't mammals and have no nipples, so they modified spiracles to secrete this milk. Compositionally it's high in protein, not all that different from mammalian milk, and cloudy white in color. A few years ago European scientists tried to pitch it as the next superfood. The current problem: extracting the milk usually requires sacrificing the mother.

37:36 Fear of bugs is learned from your mother
Jessica says fear of insects is learned, not innate. A colleague at Rutgers ran an experiment: put babies and tarantulas together, and the babies aren't afraid on their own; but if the mother or primary caregiver shows disgust, the babies show disgust too. Same for snakes and other animals. She uses her own two kids as an example: her daughter didn't start daycare until nearly one and was never afraid of bugs; her son started daycare at six weeks, and the daycare teacher was afraid of bugs and would scream and try to swat them, so the son grew up afraid of bugs — even though his own mother isn't. Once this learned behavior forms, it's very hard to change.

item.title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-cn907a40-残障剧团让健全人当被歧视的少数-不是要你同情/
item.description: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied minority become the Sinners, the ones who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
item.content:encoded:
Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied minority become the Sinners, the ones who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.

Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment.

7:15 Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanyā (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, an older sister, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at holidays, what she felt was ‘like being walked like a little dog or cat’. Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These testimonies made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

11:19 Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair. When she moved, the only people she could ask for help were friends who also use wheelchairs, hauling load after load with bags hung all over the chairs. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright — they'd have finished in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance at integration at all’. That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

14:19 Writing the able-bodied as the discriminated Sinners
Leyi Theatre's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the remaining able-bodied minority, guilty of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become the Sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a situs inversus person, why not flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for — what she calls writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: a Sinner father, to spare his son from suffering for his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about Sinners and augmented humans.

22:25 How the unseen and the unheard partner up
Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled into a pairing by deaf actor Li Ning at an audition. His first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, ‘absolutely impossible to communicate’, a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign-language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

25:28 Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without any trouble — the director had no way to assess it, and only wondered how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, and could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

30:36 She received the best production award from the ICU
In 2024, Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao's heart failed and she went into the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more after finishing, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, the first integrated disability production, and the only one in the ‘Nothing Is Impossible’ section.

35:45 After writing this play, she changed her answer on being born
The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families: deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you won't be able to hear either; a husband who deceives his wife into having a child; a family that favours boys over girls; and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice in the matter.

36:45 The same question, and Cai Cong answers it the opposite way
The episode sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume, merely because the child might also be visually impaired, that such a life was not worth starting — they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument around this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose does it actually have.

item.title: Inheritance of acquired traits is proven in C. elegans, not yet in humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-huberman-获得性遗传在线虫已被证实-人类还没有证据/
item.description: Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in C. elegans, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.
item.content:encoded:
Textbooks use the Weismann barrier to explain why the muscles you build can't be passed down; but in C. elegans, knock out the offspring's own ability to make small RNAs and they still resist viruses their parents encountered — changing only RNA in the brain alters behavior three generations later.

35 minutes walks the whole conceptual chain from DNA to small RNAs, with experimental designs and key numbers included; on the mammalian part the speaker repeatedly states what is unknown, so no transferable conclusions are handed to you.

4:37 The genome is the whole book, and each cell pulls out one page
Every cell carries the same genome. Rechavi's analogy is that every room holds an IKEA manual with instructions for building everything in the house; but the kitchen needs different things than the bathroom, so each cell pulls out one page, and that page is RNA, and the furniture assembled from it is protein. The messenger RNA that actually encodes protein is only a small part of RNA: less than 2% of the genome's sequence encodes messenger RNA, while a great deal of transcribed RNA does other things, much of it still not understood. This distinction is the foundation for everything that follows — DNA determines which instructions can be opened, and only then does the question arise of whether lived experience can rewrite those instructions.

11:35 Two barriers block the inheritance of acquired traits
Why, by default, can't what you learn in life be passed on? Rechavi attributes it to two barriers. The first is the separation of soma and germline: in the 19th century August Weismann proposed what is now called the Weismann barrier — only germ cells can hand information to the next generation, and what happens in the rest of the body should stay in the body; this barrier has been called biology's second law, the first being natural selection. The second is epigenetic reprogramming: genetic material accumulates all kinds of chemical modifications, but in sperm and eggs, and in the early embryo, these modifications are largely erased — roughly 90% in mammals and humans. The reason for the erasure is to return to the original manual, preserving the potential to build all the furniture rather than being locked into the few pieces one room happened to make.

12:46 It was opposed and also wanted, and not only for data reasons
This barrier theory kept acquired inheritance out of favor for a long time. Rechavi describes two sides: one is theory, the barrier is simply there; the other is the atmosphere the controversy itself creates. He gives Schrödinger's 1944 book as an example — Schrödinger wrote that acquired inheritance doesn't hold up and doesn't happen, and at the same time wrote that this is sad, because natural selection is bleak: nothing you do affects the genetic information of the next generation, and all you can give your children is money and education. Rechavi says he can psychologically understand why many people want it to be true, because it gives life meaning. But he doesn't push this into ‘because people want to believe it, it has promise’; he only says RNA is a new lead, a candidate molecule that in recent years has come to the fore even in the mammalian field.

16:20 C. elegans can run hundreds of generations in one PhD
Why trust C. elegans? Rechavi's list of conditions is very concrete: a C. elegans worm always has 959 cells, 302 of them neurons, and since the 1980s it has had a complete connectome, like a subway map marking who talks to whom; the body is transparent, so you can watch neurons fire directly, and you can switch genes on and off with optogenetics; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced, earlier than humans; each mother produces about 250 nearly genetically identical offspring, raised in a petri dish eating bacteria, in a highly controlled environment where nature and nurture can be separated; generation time is 3 days, so one PhD can run through hundreds of generations of worms. Under these conditions, he says, the inheritance of acquired traits in C. elegans already has very clear, indisputable evidence, and almost no one in the epigenetics field disputes it.

21:20 Offspring that can't make small RNAs still resist viruses
The experimental design is clean enough to read by color: use a fluorescent virus, and if the virus replicates successfully the worm turns green, while if it is destroyed the worm stays black. First let worms be infected by a virus and destroy it, then knock out the machinery for making small RNAs in their offspring — these offspring cannot make small RNAs from scratch themselves. Then infect them with the same virus. If they still stay black, the only explanation is that they inherited small RNAs from their parents. That is exactly what happens: all the offspring stay black, and the resistance can be passed on for several more generations. Sequencing can directly read those small RNAs matching the viral genome, and only offspring whose parents were infected have them. These worms have no T cells or B cells; they defend against viruses with RNA, and this mechanism is RNA interference, which won the Nobel Prize in 2006.

24:46 The brain and inheritance don't speak the same language
The boldest question in this episode is: can the brain leave information for the next generation? Rechavi points out the obstacle is translation — the brain stores information in the three-dimensional structure of synaptic connections, while any heritable information must squeeze through the bottleneck of a single cell, the fertilized egg. He also offers another possibility: learning something may just mean removing a particular odor receptor, in which case one RNA controlling that receptor would be enough to pass it on; such phenomena have been reported in mammals, but he says they haven't been proven convincingly enough, because no one has explained how information gets from the brain to the germ cells. His own route bypasses translation: in a 2019 Cell paper, changing only the production of naturally occurring small RNAs in the worm's brain altered the foraging behavior of offspring, affecting them all the way to three generations later, with the mechanism landing on the germline gene sage-2, and also requiring the protein that physically carries RNA.

28:17 Mammals lack an RNA amplifier
Why can C. elegans do it while mammals must be doubted? Rechavi's mechanism is blunt: the worm's secret is that it can keep amplifying these small RNAs, so the signal doesn't get diluted. In mammals there is no known comparable amplification mechanism, so the question becomes — how does a tiny bit of RNA affect the whole organism? One possibility is that it acts only very early in development: when there are only a few cells, perhaps even acting on the placenta formed during pregnancy, and from there gradually steers development off course, with problems like metabolism following. This is the ‘developmental origins of health and disease’ line of thinking. He also frames RNA's role in mammals as a candidate rather than a conclusion: small RNAs are the leading candidate for transmitting protective or harmful effects of stress, but ‘in mammals we don't know, and time will tell’.

31:07 RNA is more plastic than DNA, so start with diagnostics
The applications come in three layers. The nearest is diagnostics: in Israel, most couples preparing to have children get DNA diagnostics for genetic diseases, but right now no one looks at RNA; if the mechanism becomes clearer, RNA would be another layer, a whole new world, and there may be certain RNAs associated with disease. The advantage is that it isn't fixed the way DNA is — DNA is yours, and if you can't change it you can only choose another embryo; RNA is plastic. Only a step further out is intervention: in rodent experiments, overfeeding causes problems in the next generation, but if the mice are made to exercise, this abnormal inheritance is corrected; when doing IVF, perhaps you could change the RNA composition of the things you introduce. Rechavi is restrained about the timeline: he says this doesn't happen now, it's science fiction, but if it were figured out, he has imagined telling someone preparing for IVF ‘you should go run on the treadmill for a while’, and that would change your RNA profile.

item.title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail. Retail Theft Is Now an Industry
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-oddlots-偷来的货能卖到原价七八折-零售盗窃已经产业化/
item.description: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
item.content:encoded:
Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the identifiers and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.

High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorized, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the state of federal legislation — with plenty of hard numbers.

8:19 A third of shrink is self-inflicted
Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious — in Scott's phrasing, the things we do to ourselves and the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years is that of malicious shrink, roughly 40% comes from internal employees, 35% from people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational loss. These percentages move only a few points a year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that they have been underreported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capture it.

22:52 Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to trade for money — so they get physical, and they have gotten physical. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. That's why asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he'd trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

23:53 RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and is still expensive and hard to scale in 2026. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, effectively a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you have to use active-signal solutions. He also says tag cost is now essentially zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely expensive. They've tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but retrofitting an entire production line for a single drill is very hard to scale.

25:58 Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
The division of labor works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs to go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a small crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a carve-out that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backward from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

35:19 One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross-margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little money, locking up pencils out. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and when they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon an associate, and the average unlock takes 90 seconds; locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rose, because the product was finally in stock.

39:23 A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
On the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion — whole containers get rerouted at the port or transload warehouse and hauled somewhere else, even loaded back onto a container ship and sailed away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, with AI making the documents look real, and the driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new may not be the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the piece that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get cracked open by a crowd; and the other side has good intelligence, they don't touch every car, only the one carrying guns or electronics.

41:28 AI in security is an efficiency tool
Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency problem: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a suspicious combination of behaviors and then identify the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

44:30 Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
He says he's very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan cosponsors, it has passed the House, and it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, with the president saying he'll sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination center. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalization and defunding the police.

item.title: Baseball's stadium music isn't accompaniment — it's how fans take the game back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-throughline-棒球场的音乐不是伴奏-是球迷抢回比赛的方式/
item.description: Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.
item.content:encoded:
Baseball's official historian thinks stadium music is too loud, but it was fans singing Hey Hey Goodbye in unison that rattled the opposing pitcher — music turns spectators into part of the game.

Medium information density: the first half is baseball music history, and only the second half, the Nancy Faust story, is worth the price. Worth listening for anyone into sports, live experience, or fan culture.

0:00 One walk-up song can turn a passerby into a fan
Host Randa Abdel Fattah says she was indifferent to baseball for most of her life, until Mets pitcher Edwin Diaz's walk-up song Narco in 2022 changed that. Diaz is a closer, usually entering at a key moment in the late innings, and the team uses his walk-up song to announce to the opponent that the fun is over and this one is ours. The entrance video went viral, the team started handing out plastic trumpets to fans, mascots Mr. and Mrs. Met pretended to play them, and eventually the team flew the original artist, Timmy Trumpet, in from Australia to perform live. The host says that if you were in the stands at that moment, the feeling was electric.

6:18 The official historian thinks the ballpark is too loud
MLB's official historian John Thorne says plainly that he doesn't like entrance music. What he misses is the quiet between half-innings — quiet that makes other sounds louder and clearer: the strange sound of a bat hitting a baseball, the same sound when Babe Ruth hit, and when Josh Gibson hit; the dull thud of a leather glove catching a fly ball; a coach yelling at a player to keep running and steal second. He thinks nonstop audio and the endless fight for fans' attention may have robbed a kid who goes to the ballpark to dream of that right.

10:31 Take Me Out was originally a women's suffrage song
The seventh-inning stretch was originally literal: stand up, move your legs, get the blood flowing. It became a musical moment thanks to a 1908 song, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, which was actually about women's suffrage. The protagonist in the original lyrics is named Katie Casey, a baseball fan who knows all the players' names, gets upset when the umpire makes a bad call, and knows what to do when the score is tight — she gets the whole crowd to sing along. From this a new genre, the "baseball song," was born, flooding sheet music, cylinder records and 78s in the 1910s.

12:35 The baseball song boom was publishers, not fans
John Thorne points out that the 1910s wave of baseball music was less about fans liking it than publishers liking it — it was essentially a marketing tool to pull people into the ballpark. The evidence is the number of copycats: George M. Cohan released Take Your Girl to the Ball Game almost the same week, followed by imitations like I Want to Go to the Ball Game. But despite Tin Pan Alley producing so many baseball songs, large-scale singing in actual ballparks remained rare, and John says the main reason was technical: sound systems were too primitive, and before radio took hold, a brass band was still the best accompaniment.

17:47 That 1977 singalong broke the opposing pitcher
On a muggy July night in Chicago in 1977, the White Sox were down two runs to the Kansas City Royals. After the White Sox put runners on first and second, people in the stands started singing Hey Hey Goodbye, louder and louder, until more than 45,000 fans joined in and the announcer had to raise his voice to be heard over the singing. The White Sox then exploded — bases loaded, cleared, four runs in — and the other side was forced to change pitchers. As the pitcher walked off the mound, Chicago fans "saw him off" even louder. Nancy Faust says what she was thinking was "did I hear that right," because this wasn't the kind of thing you normally heard at a ballpark — it was more like mockery.

23:51 She gave players songs, fans fed her ideas
In her first years with the White Sox, Nancy Faust still played a set repertoire: the national anthem, Take Me Out to the Ball Game, and the hour when the crowd came in. In her third year she started improvising, playing whatever she saw. When Dick Allen came up, the crowd would leave the restrooms and popcorn stands, so she played the then-popular Jesus Christ Superstar, and when he hit a home run the place went crazy. Fans sitting around her booth started offering her ideas: one player used to work at a watch counter, got stuck there when the store closed, so when he came up she played Does Anybody Really Know What Time It Is. She says she was "the soundtrack to everything that was happening," not just to the players.

25:52 An opposing pitcher admitted the singing shook his confidence
After that 1977 singalong, one opposing pitcher told reporters: you're standing on the mound, there are men on base, Zisk is in the batter's box, thirty thousand people are singing Kiss It Goodbye, and that shakes your confidence. Nancy Faust later read in a book that players recalling those years said they hated hearing that sound, and cringed when they heard na-na-goodbye. And White Sox slugger Richie Zisk said of those same fans: I don't know whether they came to see us or we came to see them, but I can tell you it fired us up. Nancy's conclusion: I guess I did have an impact, I just didn't know it at the time.

28:56 She can't read music, it's all by ear
Every song Nancy Faust improvised over her career, she did by ear — she can't read music. Hum a few bars of anything and within seconds she'd play it back on the organ. She retired from the White Sox organist job in 2010, White Sox fan and former President Barack Obama personally wrote to congratulate her on her career, and the booth she sat in for decades is now named after her. She still occasionally comes back for special occasions, like Pope Night, playing Gotta Have Faith and Don't Stop Believing.

item.title: Iron Age Ireland had no Celtic invasion, only trade and language
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-10-ancients-爱尔兰铁器时代没有凯尔特人入侵-只有贸易和语言/

item.description: The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.
item.content:encoded:
The traditional story says Celts brought iron to Ireland around 500 BC, but archaeology finds almost no trace of incoming migrants — Celtic identity was really a language community that grew slowly out of a Late Bronze Age maritime trade network.

Medium information density, with a long setup in the first half. The real value is in the second half, on Celtic identity, sacral kingship and the Fianna warband, suited to listeners interested in pre-Roman Europe.

2:18 Why the Irish Iron Age is the murkiest period
John Waddell says the Irish Iron Age is the darkest stretch of Irish prehistory, partly because the people of the time cremated their dead. In much of Europe people were buried with large quantities of fine grave goods, whereas cremation followed by burial destroys a great deal of useful archaeological evidence. So despite fine metalwork and monuments, the absence of burial evidence makes this period especially hard to read. He also points out that using the phrase "Celtic Iron Age" to describe the period amounts to slapping an ethnic label on an era, adding another layer of trouble to an already complicated story.

9:28 Sea routes connected people rather than isolating them
Waddell repeatedly stresses an underrated fact: in prehistory, waterways were channels connecting people, not barriers. Ireland and Britain are both islands, and people habitually assume islands mean isolation, but coastal routes and river routes were very likely the main means of connection. Before the Romans built straight roads, travel by water was far easier than travel by land. This means we have consistently underestimated how connected the populations of prehistoric Britain and Ireland were. The Irish Sea itself was a connecting force, and the English Channel linked England to the continent.

10:31 Sacred sites sat on high ground, not by rivers
Tristan asks whether Iron Age settlements were all near rivers and coasts. Waddell's answer is unexpected: famous sites like Tara, Rathcroghan and Navan Fort are not obviously on major routes. Each sits on high ground in its own different way, and these locations may have carried a kind of sanctity since the Neolithic. Tara was already an important burial place before 3000 BC, and its story runs into the Middle Ages, representing more than 4000 years of ritual activity. The importance of these places comes from accumulated time and religious meaning, not from rivers and sea routes.

15:38 A sacred king who fails or is wounded is deposed
Waddell draws a key concept out of medieval Irish texts: sacral kingship. The king of Tara was not a political strongman; his fundamental duty was to maintain cosmic order. If a sacred king could not bring good harvests, he was deposed. Another feature was that his body had to be flawless: once a sacred king was wounded, scarred or deformed, he was deposed. Waddell thinks this ritual may eventually be traceable in the archaeology of Britain and Ireland, suggesting that in the Celtic era, the pre-Roman period, certain tribal rulers did carry a sacred quality.

21:43 The Celts were not invaders but a language community
The traditional story is that around 500 BC, Celtic-speaking peoples brought knowledge of iron to Ireland. Waddell says this is wrong. His best definition of the ancient Celts is "people who spoke Celtic", not an ethnic or racial definition. Ireland in the pre-Roman period was undoubtedly Celtic-speaking, but archaeology finds almost no evidence of immigrants in the Iron Age or the Late Bronze Age. Instead, from around 1000 BC there is abundant archaeological evidence of trade and exchange between Britain and Ireland, with the Thames, the Rhine, the Rhône, the Saône, the Ruhr and the Danube all serving as major corridors. Trade and exchange means movement of people, and people carried myths, legends and language with them. The Celtic languages most likely took shape gradually amid this Late Bronze Age surge of connectivity.

31:04 The Banquet Hall is actually a ritual processional way
On the hill of Tara there is a monument called the "Banquet Hall", a pair of very long parallel earthworks. Waddell's colleague Conor Newman established that it was never a banquet hall — it is far too large to be any kind of hall. Standing between the banks, you find you cannot see the world outside, because the banks are still high even in their ruined state. Newman proposed that it was a processional way running from the northern end of the hill to the centre of the summit, used for royal inauguration rituals. There are gaps in the banks that let the procession look left and right at the burials and other monuments on either side, reminding the man about to become sacred king of the stories of his ancestors and predecessors. Waddell compares it to Rome's Appian Way, lined on both sides with tombs.

33:07 Beneath Tara lies a timber circle bigger than Stonehenge
Geophysical survey on the hill of Tara revealed a huge circular timber structure, four to five times the scale of Stonehenge. It was built around 2000 BC and would have stood on the hilltop as prominently as Stonehenge does, yet today there is no trace of it on the ground — only a faint outline of the circle visible in aerial photographs. Waddell says this reminds us that large timber circles older than Stonehenge are a feature of the prehistoric landscape of Britain and Ireland. Tara's burials have another detail: many of them intersect one another, as if new graves were deliberately laid partly over old ones to connect with ancestral remains, both legitimising one's own existence and conveying some kind of story.

39:22 The forgotten king Dathi and a Swiss myth
Waddell tells the story of an almost forgotten king, Dathi, associated with Rathcroghan in western Ireland. In medieval legend Dathi was the last pagan king of Ireland, said to have campaigned on the European continent, perhaps reaching the foot of the Swiss Alps, and to have been struck dead by lightning at the foot of the Alps, with his body carried back to Ireland and buried at Rathcroghan. The story was especially popular in the 19th century, because some people took it as proof that Irish military power reached far overseas. But Waddell says it looks like pure fabrication: there was never any Irish invasion of Switzerland. Dathi most likely only raided Britain occasionally. He was later overshadowed by the more famous warrior Cú Chulainn and gradually forgotten.

item.title: Ashurbanipal's Library: He Was Both a Tyrant and the Earliest Book Collector
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-stuffmissed-亚述巴尼拔的图书馆-他既是暴君-也是最早的藏书家/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Ashurbanipal locked defeated kings in dog kennels and forced people to make bricks from their ancestors' bones — and he also built humanity's earliest systematic library, keeping the Epic of Gilgamesh alive to this day.

Medium information density; the first half is Mesopotamian background, and the second half — how the library was preserved and deciphered — is where the value is.

0:01 One man, two completely opposite first impressions
At the British Museum, Tracy read the display panels on Ashurbanipal's library and thought, "this man's library is astonishing"; in the same gallery Patrick read the other panels about him as king of Assyria and came away thinking, "this man was truly cruel." The same body of material can support two entirely opposite impressions at once, and the rest of the episode picks apart that contradiction: he really did yoke the defeated king of Elam to his chariot and shut a rival in a dog kennel, and he really did order texts from across the empire copied and sent to the capital.

4:04 You cannot lay out a timeline for Mesopotamia at all
Tracy wanted to open the episode with a basic timeline and found she couldn't. Mesopotamia spans more than three thousand years from the first cities, with civilizations, kingdoms and empires overlapping and influencing one another, so a linear timeline is itself a distortion. Assyrian history is divided into the Early Assyrian period (from about 2600 BCE), the Old Assyrian (from about 2025 BCE), the Middle Assyrian (from about 1363 BCE) and the Neo-Assyrian (911 to 609 BCE), followed by a post-empire period. Assyrians still exist today: roughly three to five million people in Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey identify as Assyrian.

9:10 His father split the empire in two to prevent civil war
Esarhaddon's father Sennacherib had Babylon utterly destroyed and even diverted canals to flood the ruins, and was later assassinated by his own sons — read as divine punishment for destroying Babylon. Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and positioned himself as its "governor" rather than its king. In 672 BCE he divided his two sons' roles: Shamashumukin would govern Babylon, and Ashurbanipal was made crown prince of Assyria. The arrangement was meant to prevent a repeat of the civil war that had attended his own accession. The episode says explicitly that this will come back later — because the brothers eventually turned on each other.

9:10 He got an education a king was not supposed to get
Ashurbanipal's education had already begun when he was made crown prince. He learned horsemanship, chariot driving, archery, military tactics and court etiquette — the standard royal package. But he also studied literature and history, knew multiple Sumerian and Akkadian dialects, and could read and write cuneiform. The episode stresses that kings of this era were not usually educated this academically, and often were not literate at all — literacy was the business of scholars and scribes. The likely reason he got this education is that early in life he was not being raised fully as the heir to the throne.

13:14 In the reliefs, he wears a writing tool at his belt
Ashurbanipal was a patron of the arts, building temples and palaces and commissioning vast numbers of reliefs. Many depict him in battle, lion hunting, or going about daily life amid wealth and luxury, and some show the severed heads of enemies. The episode singles out one detail: in many depictions he wears a writing stylus at his belt, including in scenes where he is killing lions with a sword — Holly jokes that he may have wanted to write a diary entry after killing a lion. The reliefs of his reign are regarded as the peak of Assyrian art, and the lion-hunt reliefs are now in the British Museum.

15:19 Cruelty was not his invention — he took it to an extreme
The episode draws a clear distinction: practices like displaying enemies' severed heads were the norm among rulers of ancient Mesopotamia; but in the depictions he himself commissioned and in the records others left, Ashurbanipal is seen as having pushed this to an extreme. Specific examples include: salting the land after putting down a revolt, forcing people to grind up their ancestors' bones to make bricks for a palace, making the defeated king of Elam pull his chariot in a triumph, and forcing one rival to live in a dog kennel. About that rival, some accounts say he was forced to wear a dog collar, others that a chain was run through his jaw.

21:39 This was the earliest systematically collected library
The library was built in the capital, Nineveh, and tablets have been found in the Southwest Palace, the North Palace, and around the temples of Ishtar and Nabu. The episode stresses two things: first, it is unclear whether these were the library's original storage locations or the result of tablets scattering after the city's destruction; second, this is one of the earliest known libraries to be systematically acquired and organized — a deliberately collected, curated repository of knowledge, and the largest collection of Assyrian texts in the world. Excavations yielded more than twenty thousand tablets and fragments, many bearing standardized colophons, indicating a systematic method of labelling and cataloguing. The total number of complete tablets is in fact unknown.

22:39 He ordered the whole empire to hand over texts, and knew who to ask
Ashurbanipal ordered temples and palaces across the empire to send texts to Nineveh, usually by having a copy made, with him receiving the copy or the original. Surviving documents show he actually wanted the originals, and that subordinates may have "creatively misinterpreted" the instructions in order to keep originals in their own temples or collections. Surviving correspondence also shows he knew exactly where to look for the texts he wanted, and who might hold works he did not know about but that were worth acquiring. Holly describes him as having a network of scholarly acquisition librarians. Some texts in the library were written by him, and many tablets carry colophons in his hand.

item.title: There are no irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable luck
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-tyler-没有不可替代的领袖-只有不可替代的运气/
item.description: Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born on the wettest steppe in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.
item.content:encoded:
Diamond says history has no irreplaceable leaders — Genghis Khan just happened to be born on the wettest steppe in two thousand years. But people like Rachel Carson and Resnick really did move things forward by ten or twenty years.

Diamond is 89, talking about leaders, geographic determinism, Papua New Guinea and Bach cantatas. Medium information density, but the back half — on environmental optimism and writing method — is where the value is.

1:09 There are no irreplaceable leaders, only irreplaceable timing
Diamond's answer to ‘who is the most irreplaceable leader in human history’ is ‘no one.’ Not because leaders don't matter, but because time washes out the differences: Jesus was a charismatic founder, but the Roman Empire of the same period had half a dozen other prophets; Genghis Khan built the largest land empire from China to Poland, but recent research found that the wettest period on the steppe in the past two thousand years fell right around his birth — had he been born twenty years earlier or two hundred miles farther away, we would never have known his name. From this Diamond distinguishes two kinds of questions: why you and I speak English right now has its answer in the domesticable plants and animals of the Fertile Crescent, nothing to do with individuals; why Amazon is what it is today has its answer in Bezos alone.

13:50 Rachel Carson moved the environmental movement up by ten years
Cowen challenges Diamond with the environmental Kuznets curve: once per capita income hits 28,000, countries naturally turn green — is Carson replaceable? Diamond concedes the movement would have come anyway, but stresses she at least moved it up by about ten years — the day after Silent Spring was published, a senator announced a government investigation into toxic chemicals. More crucial was her position at the time: back then a professional scientist writing popular science was seen as ‘selling out,’ and she was not a university professor, so no one could say that of her; she was a woman, wrote like a poet, and would read her drafts aloud to hear them. Diamond says that even today's best science writer, Richard Dawkins, doesn't write as well as she did.

18:00 The pomegranate juice industry waited five thousand years to appear
Cowen tests Diamond's replaceability theory with the pomegranate juice industry: without the Resnick family, America would eventually have gone down this road anyway. Diamond says no. Pomegranates were domesticated five or six thousand years ago, but there was never a global pomegranate juice industry, because pomegranate juice is extremely hard to make — you cut an orange and squeeze, but the pomegranate's value is inside an extremely hard rind, and the contents are not pulp but small seeds; scaled production requires a three-story-tall tower that crushes whole pomegranates rind and all. In 2002 America had 22 pomegranate growers, 21 of them small farmers with no money and no motive. Lynda Resnick put in about two hundred million dollars and waited 18 years before turning a profit. Companies like Coca-Cola and Nestlé would never allow a division to invest 150 million dollars and lose money for 18 years.

29:32 Face-to-face social skill is in cliff-edge decline
Diamond's advice to a 25-year-old who wants to become influential: learn to talk to people face to face, put down indirect communication tools.
