He has done 60 years of fieldwork in Papua New Guinea, and saw Chevron bring in international lawyers from Switzerland to negotiate with villagers who had never left their village — the lawyers thought they'd close it in a day, but the agreement reached on day one, the villagers said on day two, ‘we forgot that agreement, the people who signed it don't count, these are a few other negotiators.’ The villagers had negotiated face to face their whole lives, with far more skill than the international lawyers. Diamond says that over the past 40 to 50 years he has watched social skills degrade, and in his 39-year-old child's generation it is especially striking, because most communication is no longer face to face and people no longer understand each other.

33:54 New Guineans may be smarter than Westerners
Diamond answers ‘yes’ outright, and says some people hate him for it. His argument is that natural selection pushed in different directions: over the past ten thousand years European survival depended mainly on surviving infectious diseases like smallpox, tuberculosis and measles, with little to do with intelligence; the main causes of death in New Guinea were coping with an extremely difficult environment and coping with other New Guineans — warfare there was constant. So his impression is that New Guineans on average ask more questions and are smarter. He adds that Westerners usually think they are stupid because they use stone tools — but they lack metal tools because agricultural output was far lower, not because of intelligence. Cowen presses him on a Nature paper claiming West Eurasians have gotten smarter since the Stone Age; Diamond says he hasn't seen it, but for more than a century eugenicists have been trying to prove Europeans are smarter, with no evidence at all.

39:24 The Industrial Revolution happened in Britain because it is an island
Diamond rejects Greg Clark's hypothesis that the British became more patient by intermarrying and lowering their time preference. His explanation is geography: Britain is an island, needs no standing army, and is not constantly invaded — the last successful invasion was 1066. Not needing an army, it gradually developed democracy, and democracy is a productive form of government. Britain also sits on the Atlantic coast, and like the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal, is one of the countries that could spread across the world, because the Atlantic coast was the testing ground for seafaring technology. He mentions that in the 1600s Britain cut off its king's head and Parliament became powerful. As for Daron Acemoglu and Jim Robinson's extractive vs inclusive institutions theory, Diamond says he has learned more from Jim Robinson than from any individual in the past 20 years, but thinks they give geography less weight than he does.

44:32 Big business and young people have made him cautiously optimistic
Diamond says that 20 years ago he would have said the most evil and destructive force in the world was big business, which back then basically didn't care about the environment. But over the past 20 years big business has come to care more and more: Walmart leads on sustainable products, Unilever leads on sustainable fisheries, even oil companies. In 1999 the World Wildlife Fund sent him to do an environmental study of Chevron's oil field in Papua New Guinea; he expected it to be terrible, but found Chevron extremely cautious, because they knew that if they screwed up, New Guineans would sue them, and they wouldn't get the Norwegian oil field development contract either. Another source of optimism is young people: 25 years ago young people didn't care about the environment, now they care very much. The probability he gives is 51% good outcome, 49% bad.

47:46 The most important question is not to find the most important question
Cowen asks what the biggest environmental problem is at the global macro level, and Diamond laughs and says this is why interviewing Diamond is frustrating: his answer is always ‘the most important thing is not to go looking for that one most important thing, because the world is complicated.’ He uses marriage as an analogy: a couple about to marry asks what the single most important thing for a happy marriage is, and the answer is not to go looking for that one most important thing — you need to get 37 things right, and if you get 36 right but disagree on sex or religion, the marriage breaks. Back to the question itself, he says there are three things we must get right: climate change, inequality, and nuclear risk — including the risk of nuclear war and nuclear winter.

item.title: AI Is a Rounding Error for Ordinary People: Diffusion Takes Fifty Years, Backlash Won't Wait
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-09-interconnects-ai-对普通人是舍入误差-扩散要五十年-反弹却等不了/
item.description: The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is coming too fast.
item.content:encoded:
The Industrial Revolution gave ordinary people cheap clothes and sewing machines; AI so far gives them fun images and better search — the benefits are too indirect, and the political backlash is coming too fast.

An eight-minute short take, not especially dense, but it offers a counterintuitive angle: AI's biggest risk isn't technical failure, it's that ordinary people can't feel the benefits.

0:00 AI is still a rounding error in daily life
The author spent a few weeks on his honeymoon without touching AI at all, and on returning realised: the points where ordinary people encounter AI are either marginal or confusing. The positive impressions are making fun images and an enhanced Google search; the negative ones are addictive social media algorithms, a friend of a friend hooked on AI chatbots, and various claims about data centers. Family, food, transport, entertainment — the core of daily life — have barely changed directly. His conclusion: being fascinated by AI is the result of a very small number of people actively choosing it, and only by stepping outside the bubble do you see that what's happening today really doesn't matter that much to most people.

0:00 The Industrial Revolution gave physical things; AI gives indirect benefits
The first Industrial Revolution brought cheaper clothes, cookware, reading material and new livelihoods; the second brought sewing machines, food preservation, indoor plumbing, photography, better light sources, bicycles and electrification — a long list, and a very physical one. The author worries that even if AI's benefits materialise (new scientific discoveries, treatments for rare diseases, sustained economic abundance), they are too indirect: ordinary people won't credit OpenAI or Anthropic with saving their life, because it was their family doctor who told them about the new treatment; and not many Americans will care that OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. He judges that fifty years from now, the daily life of the average American will still look a lot like today.

3:47 AI today is mainly a tool serving elites
Knowledge work is about half the US economy, and for that half AI is already (or soon will be) as foundational as electricity; rapid agent improvements over the next eighteen months will accelerate this. But a transformative, highly productive tool that only lifts half of society is highly unstable. The author cites the "Engels' pause": from 1790 to 1840 British workers' wages stagnated while GDP per capita grew rapidly amid technological upheaval. He argues that if the AI industry itself thinks this is the closest analogy, then backlash from those who don't benefit is legitimate. He also agrees with Doug O'Laughlin's judgment: knowledge work output explodes while headcount in the tech industry very likely shrinks.

3:47 The backlash isn't rooted in AI, it's Big Tech's old debts
The author splits the political backlash facing AI into two layers: first, early positive impacts are too indirect; second, it is deeply intertwined with Western society's historical grievances against Big Tech. He stresses that the latter merely collided with AI in time — if AI's exponential growth had happened decades after the growing pains of platforms like Google and Meta, the data center issue very likely would never have risen to such a central political position. Solving either one would substantially relieve the pressure and give the industry more time to show positive reasons. And AI itself, through doom rhetoric and declarations of mass unemployment, has marked itself as a negative or unsafe technology, making both harder.

3:47 Robots might rescue the narrative for LLMs
The author raises an ironic possibility: if the intelligence explosion from mass-producing large language models spills over into robotics and accelerates the spread of robots in daily life, humans will quickly grasp AI's tangible benefits. This is ironic because many people have been working hard to convince the public that this LLM wave is very different from the general AI progress of the past ten or twenty years. If in the end the same dynamic saves (or largely drowns out) the LLM narrative, that would be funny. He also cautions that the connection between robotics, autonomous driving and the current AI revolution is currently more a matter of storytelling.

3:47 Diffusion takes fifty years; the fight against it won't wait
The author calls the present the first five years of a fifty-year diffusion process, and lays out two simple problems: the positive impacts are too indirect, and political backlash is entangled with Big Tech's history. He judges that the story of diffusion will be far longer than the struggle against it. Young people paying attention today will, within their lifetimes, see powerful AI go from effectively 0% to over 90% full adoption. What truly marks AI's evolution is the kind deeply integrated into enterprises and acting as a personal assistant; it is only just becoming viable, and adoption will be far slower than for easily understood applications like ChatGPT. So continuing to push the technology forward is crucial — the benefits are astonishing but not a given, and there is still a great deal of hard work to do on distributing them widely.

item.title: Grok Bot in a Month: Small Teams Hide in a Cave, Big Teams Sand Off the Micro-Decisions
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-lennys-grok-bot-一个月做出来-小团队躲进山洞-大团队会拖没微决策/
item.description: Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that's shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.
item.content:encoded:
Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, but users can smell three visions sharing one screen — that's shipping your org chart. So Grok Bot started from zero, a handful of people hid in a cave for a month.

The first half is the trade-off detail of product decisions; the second half — that a bot should have its own computer, that automation shouldn't have a UI — is worth more.

0:02 Shipping a hit in a month came from a small team hiding in a cave
Grok Bot didn't start as a tab added to Cursor. It started as a team of "a handful of people" isolated in a corner of the office with a private Slack channel, going from first line of code to an internally usable prototype in about a month. Roman's judgment: with a big team and a 6-to-12-month vision plan, you wouldn't build the thing that actually shipped — because every day is a pile of non-obvious micro-decisions, and a big team sands those decisions away.

9:07 Not putting it in Cursor: users can smell three visions on one screen
Building knowledge work into Cursor isn't obviously wrong, and the team discussed it seriously. Roman says the problem with that path is "small paper cuts": the product feels oppressive to non-technical users, plus the brand association. He called out the competitor approach of "a tab for every new form factor" — users can feel that this isn't one unified vision of work but three visions sharing a screen, like "shipping your org chart." So they decided to start completely from zero.

11:08 Two or three hundred manual onboardings, so tomorrow's mistake doesn't repeat
The team personally onboarded two or three hundred people, including the host. The first few were painful: the computer wouldn't start, the user was visibly confused, and the core team had to sit on that 20-minute call. Roman says the effect of that presence is "that can never happen again" — it has to be fixed tomorrow, because tomorrow you onboard the next person. The pattern lasted about two weeks.

12:08 They deliberately didn't tell users what bots to build
Internally the pattern emerged on its own first: "5 to 10 bots each owning a slice." By the end of the second week people were promoting a standout bot to primary personal assistant, then making it chief of staff to dispatch tasks to other bots — there was even a screenshot of a user telling a bot it got promoted, and the bot asking whether that came with a raise and a bigger token budget. The team noticed, but deliberately didn't steer it during onboarding, afraid of biasing users; they wanted to see whether outside users would get there on their own. A lot of them did.

14:09 Not showing the thinking is a product stance, not laziness
Grok Bot hides a lot of internal machinery: no tool calls, no step-by-step view of what it clicks on its own computer, just a Slack-like activity indicator and on-demand stage updates. Roman's analogy: you wouldn't ask a colleague to report second by second which button he pressed and which site he visited. Some feedback did ask for a to-do list and priorities, but nobody wanted long streams of text and chain of thought — which confirmed the direction.

19:11 Those three weeks of internal beta were mostly unshipping
From internal beta to public launch was only about three weeks, and Roman says that stretch was when "we unshipped a lot": cutting experimental features, moving pseudo-developer visibility tools off the product surface — for example interfaces exposing the model's internal thinking and specific memories. The test was "what is the launch post" — if it can't be written as a convincing launch tweet, it probably shouldn't be built. He also distinguishes "Grok Bot now has" (new buttons, new dropdowns, new integrations) from "Grok Bot can now" (new capabilities); the latter is the right frame.

29:17 Automation shouldn't have a UI; 99% is generated from one sentence
Competitors' automation setup means going into a sidebar, clicking plus, picking a trigger event, picking an action. Roman calls that clunky, and the result is that people rarely actually build automations. Grok Bot's approach is to define it in natural language: tell the bot "remind me every morning at 8," and it should just do it — the user should never see the automation-creation UI. Today 99% of automations on the platform are built that way.

30:17 Two early decisions: everything in the cloud, every bot gets its own computer
Roman credits Grok Bot's success to two decisions that weren't obvious at the time. First, users should never have to think about local versus cloud, whether their computer is on, or whether starting from their phone means connecting to a machine at home — all of it in the cloud, with the bot as a persistent colleague that has its own computer and is consistent across every entry point. Second, the bot must have its own computer, because a huge number of tools have no decent MCP or API — and humans never worked through MCP and APIs anyway; they clicked pixels and typed into input boxes.

item.title: Picky Eating Isn't the Food's Fault: Fix the Relationship, Then Talk Nutrition
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-secureattach-孩子挑食别怪食物-先修关系-再谈营养/
item.description: The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's first move is to work on their own relationship with food, and that is the most effective intervention a child can get.
item.content:encoded:
The feeding strategy itself matters less than how you execute it; a parent's first move is to work on their own relationship with food, and that is the most effective intervention a child can get.

Medium information density, but the health impact tiers framework and the practical advice on neutralizing food language offer direct relief to anxious parents.

5:05 The feeding anxiety starts at the nine-month checkup
Jennifer is a registered dietitian who did nontraditional work in the USDA's SNAP education program and considered herself someone who knew how to feed a child. At the nine-month checkup the doctor said her baby's weight wasn't keeping up, and she said it felt like the rug was pulled out from under her. For years afterward she worked to keep her kids on the growth curve, and her second son showed early signs of extreme pickiness. Standing in the kitchen making lunch, she realized she couldn't be the only parent struggling this hard, and in 2019 she started Kids Eat in Color, initially posting feeding tips as a hobby.

12:12 The research behind "don't pressure your kid" isn't that strong
She says "don't force your kid to eat" is a great slogan, and for some families that one line is enough. But after digging into the research on feeding pressure, she concluded it isn't as strong as dietitians or feeding experts make it out to be, and parents actually have more room to experiment. The second part of her book is devoted to "what if the standard approach doesn't work": first the general advice, then the alternatives that are considered less ideal but can be executed with reduced risk, which she calls risk reduction.

16:19 Put one small piece of green pepper on the plate five hundred times
The exposure method she teaches parents: put one small slice of green pepper on a plate full of foods the kid likes. The goal isn't to get him to eat it, but to desensitize him to its presence. It might take five hundred times before he smells it, then licks it, then throws it at his brother, then one day eats it. The precondition is that the kid is regulated — if he isn't soothed, he simply can't try something new, because he's scared by something else. So get the kid calm before he even sits down at the table.

23:22 An anxious kid has a dry mouth and a tight throat and physically can't eat
Sarah adds the neural mechanism: when anxious, the mouth goes dry, the throat tightens, there may be nausea or stomach pain — these are exactly the signs of sympathetic (fight or flight) activation, while eating requires the parasympathetic rest and digest state. In other words, if every time you come to the table it's dread and a power struggle, you are physiologically pushing the kid in the opposite direction from eating. Play, jokes and little table games work because they bring the kid into that relaxed, connected parasympathetic state, and only then do saliva and swallowing come back.

28:26 A meal can be rescued from the worst possible start
She tells a dinner from her own house: before the parents even got back to the table, the two kids were already fighting and one slammed the door to his room. They let that kid cool off in his room while the other three started eating. Fifteen or twenty minutes later he came downstairs and started eating, the whole family was laughing, everyone was eating. She says the meal ended with the siblings fighting again, but the moment of connection in the middle was real. So don't hold yourself to perfectionism — there is usually at least one good moment in a meal, and you should find it.

32:28 Sensational headlines can basically be swiped away
The first filter she gives parents: if the headline is sensational, you can be almost certain it's wrong, probably ninety percent of it is taken out of context, so keep scrolling and don't lose sleep over it. But if it's a real event — say an outbreak of diarrhea one summer, or a specific food recall — then pay attention. What she really wants to give is a tiered framework: the first tier is severe food allergies and insufficient calorie intake (ARFID, extreme pickiness, food insecurity), which can make a kid very sick or worse, and must be dealt with first.

33:29 Protein and fiber are tiers two and three, food dyes are tier four
The second tier is protein, and every meal and most snacks should have a real protein food. The third tier is fiber, because fiber trickles down: when a kid eats enough high-fiber food, he naturally eats less of the added sugar and added sodium. And food dyes, the thing most likely to make headlines, are in the fourth tier, with a very narrow impact. She says for the vast majority of kids, artificial dyes won't change their health trajectory; for the small number of sensitive kids, parents have probably already figured it out on their own. Removing dyes from the food system wouldn't solve the childhood health crisis either.

43:35 Call it a "cookie," not an "occasional food"
To help parents who don't have a healthy relationship with food, her entry point is "talk about food with facts": call foods by their names — this is a cookie, this is a sandwich, this is your chicken, this is your sugar. Don't say "this is an occasional food, this is an everyday food," don't sort your kid's food into healthy/unhealthy or good/bad, and avoid moralizing and black-and-white thinking. She says there's no evidence that black-and-white thinking directly causes eating disorders, but research has found it is very common in kids with restrictive eating disorders, and hearing that "foods are good or bad" gets embedded in their restrictive thinking.

item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the deadliest weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the deadliest weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, Taiwan and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable judgment framework, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark and the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships went everywhere, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada around the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British Navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot do without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having the cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vulnerable point. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast — oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other, pushing hard on solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to keep themselves alive.

25:50 Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is a fine thing, it means raising my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the 20th century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley is tilting to the tech Hamiltonians
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and hit to kill when struck. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the new species really worth watching is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and that is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with the most equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he visited a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; a few months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how do you get the wounded out’ — you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag a person, with a squad of drones alongside hunting the enemy drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The changes flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one that fears this kind of parameter revolution most — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet had no great battle to fight, yet was bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — once it fails, it is catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade, doing things that change facts enough without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must add Japan as a factor, is the key to the Taiwan question in the next few years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making to AI amounts to turning retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But that is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still not fully clear, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely reset it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is the sequence: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line is placed and two blood pressure cuffs are put on (arm and right leg), with EKG, EEG and EMG hooked up. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant such as succinylcholine is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement, and why the right side first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not working well, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment does not stop at just reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in a given session a patient's seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, or even longer.

20:22 We still do not know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still do not fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter change: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which can explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over consecutive treatments. Two, large hormonal fluctuations in ACTH, prolactin, TSH and others are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanism may also differ by disease (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), and for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key data are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60%, and response rates (symptoms clearly improved) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can halve the 30-day readmission rate. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Memory problems draw the most attention among side effects
ECT's most difficult side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) mostly recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it usually affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more prone to this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misread, fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often simply lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological disease can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute; they may show posturing, waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position does not fall). Because they cannot eat or drink and are immobile for long periods, malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures and even death are easy. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl mentioned earlier with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia; immunotherapy and lorazepam both failed, and she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a place to get it. His hospital does more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across states for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often do not recognize catatonia and do not dare or think to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is also part of his daily work.

item.title: A Kid Who Loses Everything Isn't Lazy — The Prefrontal Cortex Isn't Done Yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-asklisa-孩子丢三落四不是懒-是前额叶还没长好/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-asklisa-孩子丢三落四不是懒-是前额叶还没长好/
item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: A 14-year-old boy's prefrontal cortex won't finish developing until 25, so losing track of everything isn't an attitude problem. The real problem: parents whose own executive function is already stretched thin have to build a system the kid can't possibly hold up on his own.
item.content:encoded:
A 14-year-old boy's prefrontal cortex won't finish developing until 25, so losing track of everything isn't an attitude problem. The real problem: parents whose own executive function is already stretched thin have to build a system the kid can't possibly hold up on his own.

This episode is medium-density on information, but it breaks ‘executive function’ into operable mechanisms: why an alarm is more reliable than memory, why a visual timer beats a phone, why you can't push a kid on something he doesn't care about. Suited to parents anxious about the back-to-school season.

5:12 The prefrontal cortex isn't done until 25 — not even at 18
Tori defines executive function as ‘a set of behaviors and processes led by the prefrontal cortex,’ and the brain develops ‘from back to front,’ with the prefrontal cortex the last part to mature, not ‘fully cooked’ until a kid is in his twenties. So a 14-year-old boy still has ten years to grow. She points out specifically: we don't expect any high school graduate to have executive function ‘fully wrapped up’ — an 18-year-old brain just isn't at that developmental level. But many parents assume that by 10th, 11th, 12th grade the kid should ‘have it all together’ — that expectation itself is wrong.

11:24 Parents have to catch their own guilt first, then talk solutions
The mom who wrote in said ‘I see myself in him’ and wondered if it was her fault. Tori says before giving advice you have to stop, because for many parents there's a string of scary questions behind this: Did I make him this way? Will this follow him his whole life? What will he be like at 18? She also reminds us to ‘hold two things at once’: for that boy, wearing the wrong T-shirt to the first practice is the end of the world, and that feeling is real; but in the big picture, this is the textbook definition of a ‘natural consequence’ — you didn't know to bring the jersey, so there's no jersey, it feels awful, and then we go back to the drawing board and figure out how to make this happen less often. Not bypassing the discomfort, but turning the discomfort into fuel for building the system.

13:29 The system has to be simple enough to hold, with a safety net
Tori thinks of the system as ‘division of labor’: who's responsible for checking Google Classroom, who's responsible for checking the soccer team's app, while keeping a big safety net. If checking notifications is the son's job, the parent should also glance regularly to make sure nothing major slips through. Lisa shares her own approach: when her daughter ran cross-country in 10th grade, after getting an email from the coach she'd still yell from the kitchen, ‘Did you get this email?’ and wouldn't let it go until it was confirmed, sometimes just copy-pasting the content into a text to her daughter with a note, ‘Assume you saw this.’ Tori says this trick is enough for kids without major executive function issues, but many families need a more fixed, more consistent way of checking.

15:30 Don't rely on memory — rely on a 6 p.m. Sunday alarm
Ideally you'd sit down at 3 p.m. Sunday to go through the coming week, but Tori says this ‘all sounds lovely until there's a soccer game at 2 p.m. Sunday, the 3 o'clock check time has already passed, and it never happened.’ So the second layer is the safety net: set a repeating alarm on your phone for 6 p.m. every Sunday, called ‘weekly check.’ If you already did it at 3, turn this one off; if you didn't, or something else knocked it out, this reminder tells you ‘before the week takes off, you need to do this.’ Lisa presses: so it's two slots on the calendar, 3 p.m. for the theoretical doing, 6 p.m. to confirm it actually got done — but 6 p.m. doesn't rely on memory. Tori says, ‘I can't remember anything at 6 p.m. on a Sunday.’

16:30 There is no organization fairy — only lists and reminders
Tori and Lisa spent years counseling at schools and found some kids believe ‘the organization fairy will sprinkle some magic on me someday.’ Both of them react the same way: no, buddy, there is no organization fairy, she's not coming. The kids who look organized aren't organized because they remember everything — they're organized because they have lists, planners, to-do lists, reminders. Tori says this gap is ‘what we forget to fill in for our kids’ — it's not a switch that flips on by itself. And the more distractions there are (an after-school job, caring for younger siblings, managing a chronic illness), the more you need a good, simple system to support executive function that's ‘still under construction.’

19:34 Three free tools: alarms, snooze email, visual timers
Tori starts with the things that cost nothing. First, the alarm function on your phone — she set six alarms this morning herself, one of them to confirm the carpool for her son's afternoon soccer game, because ‘our kids don't drive yet.’ Before she puts her phone away at night she does a little check, asking herself: ‘What's likely to slip my mind today?’ Second, the email ‘remind me later’ function, made specifically for those ‘mark this date, it's an October thing’ emails — you can't think about October now, so let it pop back up in three weeks instead of relying on memory to go dig it up. Third, visual timers, for ‘time blindness’: for people with a poor sense of how much time has passed or how long something takes, seeing time elapse visually is enormously helpful.

27:51 The tool that helps your kid focus is the one that derails him
Lisa quotes Angela Duckworth: we generally don't put ice cream next to the broccoli. She asks: if I need the phone to keep my kid on track, but the phone is precisely the thing that derails him best, what do I do? Tori first admits adults are the same — you pick up the phone to set an alarm, get sucked into email, reply to the first text, and then ‘I spend my whole life asking: what did I come in here to do?’ She says asking kids to do this with an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex puts them at a disadvantage to begin with. Her solution is low-tech: a Time Timer, the kind with the red pie slice, battery-powered, with nothing on it that can distract you. Also, say your purpose out loud before you pick up the phone — ‘I'm picking up the phone to set this alarm’ — to ground yourself and remind yourself there's only one task on this device.

30:58 You can't push a kid on something he doesn't care about
Tori explains why executive function is ‘uneven’: bandwidth is limited, impulse control is limited, and it drops as it gets depleted, so the more important things in a day get first claim on attention — work, picking up the kids — rather than returning the library books. But the hardest question is: what if this 14-year-old simply doesn't care about school and doesn't see the risk? Tori says first find what he does care about — say, playing soccer requires a minimum GPA and not missing too many practices. Tie the requirement to what he actually cares about: if you want to keep playing, here are the things we want to see happen, and here's the structure we'll build around you. The key is that this conversation can't happen in the heat of the moment when ‘he forgot about tomorrow's test’ — it has to wait until everyone has calmed down.

item.title: Documentary director: there is no typical old age, only specific people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-cn300980-纪录片导演说-没有典型的老年-只有一个个具体的人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-cn300980-纪录片导演说-没有典型的老年-只有一个个具体的人/
item.description: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang (前浪), says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
item.content:encoded:
Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang (前浪), says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.

The first half is the two hosts talking, heavy on feeling; the second half is the director interview, packed with killed story pitches and behind-the-scenes detail, and the information density is clearly higher. Worth starting at 41 minutes.

4:08 A five-million-yuan estate, and the law fighting the will
An elderly woman with no spouse or children died in a Shanghai nursing home. While alive she had done a voluntary guardianship notarization with notary Li Chengyang, but she never made a will. Sorting through her belongings, the notary found she had left an estate of five million yuan, including a house, cash and passbooks. She had said many times orally that she wanted to donate it to society and did not want it to go to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children of relatives she had not seen in years. There was disagreement inside the notary office too; some colleagues thought the old woman's wishes should simply be respected. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 yuan of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

11:55 Whether they slept together decided whether the estate could go to her
An elderly man with a terminal illness gave voluntary guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — and he had a biological daughter. The notary office debated this fiercely, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the caregiver was merely a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man wanting to leave his estate to his nanny was, on grounds of moral propriety, acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, the matter immediately stopped conforming to propriety. The caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in fact the marriage did not exist. So it became a question of an open relationship, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of offending public morals on the basis of such a judgment.

16:02 Old people finding partners increasingly don't register the marriage
Li Kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years and never registered the marriage from beginning to end, and there was no de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: when old people re-enter relationships after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many choose not to marry. They don't necessarily say they love this person deeply; they say they want someone to keep them company, someone to take care of them, and behind that is a fairly deep need against loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness at the time, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

24:46 Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
The hosts contrast documentary with reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — for instance, knowing the audience has views about mama's boys, so they fabricate a mama's boy on screen. This destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships — every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a stance, and that stance must be the morally most correct one, then projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you side with him. Documentary works the opposite way: it shows that no one has it easy; some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see the difficulty of every one of them, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous.

34:20 The older generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but the older generation, even when expressing psychological needs, still uses somatized language — I've been sleeping badly lately, I have a bit of a headache — and will not say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a bit depressed. The host explains: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain; anyone can have a headache or a fever, and there is no stigma. Once you talk about depression and anxiety, it is a different order of stigma and pain.

43:53 The killed pitch: all she wanted was to play mahjong
Director Fan Shiguang tells a story he killed himself: the most diligent auntie in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six every evening, like going to work, but you could see no love on her face — she just asked the doctors and nurses again and again how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did they learn that her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her play. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-meter bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was ultimately not used, because the team could not find her real inner world — they only had hold of part of the facts.

52:28 Growing old together is rare, not the norm
Fan Shiguang says the team embedded in field research with roughly fifty families, across the two seasons, and found that going from youth all the way to truly growing old together to the very end is not the norm — it is rare. Most marriages are lukewarm, or even bad. He tells of the first season's episode Airen (爱人): an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife; the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialized nursing home; the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, and the hospital won't let her come because it will affect the old man's mood. After the old man is sent to hospital, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. A little over a month after he died, the old woman said through tears: I looked down on him my whole life. When I was young I was a good student and he was a poor one; my family were intellectuals and his family were workers; he insisted on pursuing me, and there was nothing I could do about it, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

1:04:18 Learning to drive at 95: one sentence strips away the right
Fan Shiguang says the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to divide into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they've gone senile — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there is the story of a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the license exam. He thought about it and realized he had unconsciously said, "Driving is nice and all, but he is 95 after all," and then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, a 95-year-old has actually been stripped of his rights — that is, he doesn't deserve it. No Ministry of Public Security law or regulation says a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in that verbal violence the right was stripped away. The episode's bullet comments were full of people saying, can this old man really drive on the road, that's so selfish, what if he hits someone — and all those worries are built on prejudice.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while also holding that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while also holding that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.

Each case gets five or six minutes laying out the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse for the first time
Can students really assert the First Amendment in class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II led more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge of allegiance daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could face fines or even jail. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6-3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students possess some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is ruled unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added "Under God" to the pledge of allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer allowed students to opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6-1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: the first experiment on our liberties should call forth the alarm; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7-2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or demonstrable substantial interference with instruction, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not become totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host says on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still make the interviewees identifiable, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5-3. The key distinction is between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": this newspaper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that school officials may exercise control over what they promote. The rights established in Tinker were thus given their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalls that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was a child, and on looking it up finds corporal punishment has still not died out in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, with one to five swats in principle; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that instance was excessive, but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning: the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by "the harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration"; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students and students with disabilities struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 A purse search needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 a 14-year-old student in New Jersey, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers and kept looking, found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing, and TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6-3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause police require, only the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Get Criticism Heard, Lead With High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the highest of any condition.
item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the highest of any condition.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism himself and lands the intervention on a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes, high information density, no vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. That worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance on tests, sports or intellectual tasks in the moment, and it makes people avoid such situations over the long run, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety doesn't come from ability — it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media surrounds you with labels from every side
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads sketches of what a group is like. People have no patience to see the full picture and the exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations in which you feel you'll be seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative, and the result is that in a diverse society, everyone is more on guard about their own identity and about what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise lifts grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend just 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the occasion to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise — which fed a positive loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → still better grades. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people are pulled back and forth between two options: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" in order to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility — it's real pressure the situation creates; when the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback land
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. The first two ways of giving it — straight criticism, or criticism preceded by a "positive cushion" — were trusted by white students but deeply distrusted by Black students. The third way added only one line: "We have high standards, because this essay is going to be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took the essay home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude says the most useful ability is realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, when in reality people worry about how you see the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, care.
