item.description: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
item.content:encoded:
Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume harder material sharpens the mind, a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.

It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms even brilliant candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After the last failure, he had visions on the road home, came to believe he was the brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around thirty million. He was not alone: examination seats fell far short of the number of candidates, many sat the exams into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who did pass: they were masters of the eight-legged essay yet knew nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young men can only drill a dead format, the country bleeds from both ends.

22:51 British civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves
The Northcote-Trevelyan Report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist judgment: under the banner of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students across the empire. Michael Coolican's No Tradesmen and No Women points out that the 1854 report reduced the most brazen buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been growing. Exams can select people — but what they test decides whether they select the able or select people like themselves.

35:58 A bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its plans save lives or destroy them. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, a crisis brewed in the first year — the shell crisis at the start of World War I being one. What actually forces correction is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a corrective mechanism crueler than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable, you first have to create a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no amount of rigor in selection can save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy notes that the real pillar of Victorian Britain was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after a run of defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys set an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned them face to face on how to command a ship. Over the following century and more, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh passed through that gate. Daisy draws out two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages. One served safety at sea, the other a layer of status — naturally the effects differed.

47:31 Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument misses the key link
Here comes the highlight: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. The gist is that whatever a age happens to teach, the best at it will necessarily be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek and the best Cherokee scholar would still be a man of parts; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it on the spot as the most practically wise speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is eloquence running away with its author, and it misses entirely that what you learn really does matter.

51:21 Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
Daisy closes out Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training are like Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them on schedule for the sake of discipline. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced through Greek and Latin before they could touch a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproven or is useless, and the winners will be rivals who let their young learn real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles until they clearly improve, then have them estimate the area of triangles — almost no transfer. If even two shapes this close show nothing, the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. From this Daisy derives a principle of exam design: to select people who can navigate, test navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practice medicine, test medicine. An exam that actually works wires its difficulty directly into the real task.

item.title: Global liquidity peaks: the more aggressively a company burned cash on AI in H1, the sooner it gets discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A rising market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are turning from rewarded to discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A rising market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are turning from rewarded to discounted.

It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
Do not read Hong Kong's low first-day break rate as a stronger market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level that a market-based mechanism would produce — meaning the money taking part in IPOs is mostly short-term speculative arbitrage, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of new listings has shrunk and an IPO-related fund has blown up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue, which shows that temporary control on the supply side has not fixed the underlying problem: Hong Kong faces the same peak in liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive on AI, the sooner you are punished
Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half — especially those that spent their free cash flow down to nothing — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the whole supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose, and inventory still able to hold up gross margin; by Q3, when inventory is exhausted and the price increases come back, the negatives will show up together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to 2000-era Cisco
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out rent-to-own deals to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into reported sales; Nvidia has now started pushing rent-to-own as well. Free cash flow in the report halved quarter on quarter, and receivables on the books are far above historical levels — which is suspected to be partly tied to the credit enhancement and collection structure that rent-to-own brings. So Nvidia may have reached the stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, which is similar to Cisco's position back then.

33:21 Primary-market money is bullets from three years ago
The answer lies in when the funds raised. The money that will be deployed into AI and robotics between H2 2025 and H1 2026 comes mainly from funds raised at the 2020-2022 market peak; through 2023-2025 they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets in a period when no one dared to and earning the most — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models and two large chips stimulated market-based money, and the mindset became: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave; it looks more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 The property policy takes households out of the funding chain
The key to recent real estate policy is not saving developers but pulling households out of the old financing loop. Buying a pre-sale home used to mean the household played the role of financier in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later; the policy pushes the chain toward a market model, so buyers get completed homes and bear only the consumer role, with risk reset back onto developers and financing institutions. The policy was chosen when prices were near the bottom in order to first stabilise the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries both followed a similar path.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
A slow bull does not come from shouting; it comes from layering market chips by duration: at the bottom, insurance takes low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips as long money that rarely trades; above that, mutual funds and index funds play a near-stabilising role; Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index at a higher layer; only at the top are retail, private funds and active managers. The new insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match on duration, yield and liquidity — institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium and short money short: you are not allowed to take ordinary people's short money and put it into ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises get bigger with each rescue, and at least one and a half bubbles
After the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks grew ever more accustomed to intervening directly in crises by printing money, and each time they moved faster. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared out during the rate-hiking cycle, but political intervention cut it short, and then came the pandemic in 2020, so a bigger wave of easing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated — today, at least one and a half bubbles have accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print more money the moment a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is inflation, rising financial assets and widening wealth inequality all at once. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face a form of long-term stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have every incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have every incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.

It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.

5:09 The scale of money laundering hasn't moved in thirty years
The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP per year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and nobody has produced a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming fact is that the ratio hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it back from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML for near-zero effect
When banks complain that KYC is too expensive, it isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF turned anti-money-laundering into a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year, enough to solve world hunger and provide clean water for everyone. Yet the system generates enormous numbers of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still run ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly feedback-driven, and almost nobody is accountable for outcomes.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes money laundering inside the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden in goods. Roughly $25 billion in cash flows into Mexico each year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, drugs and goods are imported back toward China, and the triangle is settled with misinvoiced paperwork. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch on your wrist through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets cartel supply
Each person in China has only a $50,000 annual foreign-exchange quota, while wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with the dollar cash supply from drug cartels: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos are handed to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe gambling debts; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and the drug sales that follow. Looked at as a single gambling session it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it is a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates cartel money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 A VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from auditing each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland owe no VAT, and when sold to an affiliated shell company 20% is added; that shell company re-exports the goods back to Ireland and can claim a refund from UK tax authorities for 20% that was never paid. Round and round it goes, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record notes
In the digital-payments era, cash is down to about 9% of transactions in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK notes in circulation doubled, and the U.S. is near $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult carries only a bit over $400, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. bills are abroad, but that only pushes the question past the border: nobody knows whose hands these notes are actually sitting in.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can exchange it back for goods at face value at any time, so the cash the public holds is essentially an interest-free loan. With close to $2.5 trillion of U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, you'd add roughly another percentage point. That is exactly why central banks don't want to hear anyone discuss abolishing cash.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
Suspicious activity reports were born to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports fall into a black hole; a bank that misses one can face billion-dollar fines, while getting it right earns no reward. The side effects include debanking — large numbers of people under suspicion, many of them Muslim, cut off from financial institutions. The guest's solution isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals — raising the cost of money laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but It Still Has Room for a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity for a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity for a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
Everyone is guessing whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was there to negotiate terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit looks more like carrying a message to Moscow on Trump's behalf: don't take those on-air remarks about America not caring about Europe seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Ukraine, so escalating with a probe against NATO is one option, while Trump's earlier statements that Europe is a bunch of freeloaders gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a dedicated trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account is entirely plausible, not confirming it.

21:27 Russia's army is not exhausted and can still open a limited front
Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a limited front — not tanks rolling across Poland to Paris, but something in the Baltic direction, such as blocking the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-person Ukrainian drone team destroying an entire traditional battalion is widely told, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has not trained against drones. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, but overlook that it is also one of the parties tempered by this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even save Lithuania from Poland
A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not a lack of military power but the speed of Russian advance, combined with the shadow of nuclear deterrence, which would leave allies hesitating over whether to enter and produce a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow factors exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is not quite the same as before 2022 — then, hundreds of thousands of Russian troops massing could be clearly seen on the German and Belarusian borders, and there is no such material preparation now. So the most immediate escalation may not be a conventional invasion but smaller, ambiguous attacks that can be denied (hitting a warehouse or a drone first).

23:40 Russia is using drones to test NATO's limits
At this stage, with no sign of a massed army on the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or a provocation using a captured Ukrainian drone modified for the purpose, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest notes this probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented deaths; Russian risk-taking is steadily rising, and the West has so far given no serious response. The senior European officers he speaks with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept an honorable ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only have to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on the types of weapons it can hold, and a cutoff of Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to leave Ukraine unable to defend itself; not neutral, but emasculated, so that it cannot rise again in the next stage of the war — a year, five years or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the former Ukrainian foreign minister's summary: this war will end in one of only two ways — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not an option.

31:08 Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on street support as its only ballast. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who drove drone innovation, because he needed the backing of Commander-in-Chief Syrsky; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv elites took to the streets, and the protests, small as they were, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrsky, brought in a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to bring that body under his control, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square is the election.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what actually drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is send bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to erase is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to re-educate Ukrainians, to make them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II the Soviets carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he did not even know those writers existed, because collective memory had been wiped out. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is the fear of never again that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

45:59 Half a million veterans blocked the first wave of collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be a war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that impossible can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What really kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded blows with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — we know what they look like, we know how to fight them. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.

item.title: A Child Hitting, Biting or Kicking Isn't Misbehaving — It's Reclaiming Bodily Autonomy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. A three- or four-year-old's hitting, biting and kicking is often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything — give some choice back and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. A three- or four-year-old's hitting, biting and kicking is often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything — give some choice back and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal and models the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child who hits is shouting that he has no say over his body
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than his parents: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years he could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body, my call," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say has this child had over his own life until now, and what little bit of it can be handed back?

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But the price the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to save effort, even to enjoy a taste of power; many entered education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over style of relationship. Only by seeing both sides' situations is there room to negotiate.

9:24 We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
If an adult at a party feels overloaded, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. Turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from conventions like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: a grown-up stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back to the middle of the loud party — with an adult, you'd instantly see that as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't the knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life right now? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down — so put him at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. The adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning's argument, lost sleep, and a pile of accumulated stress. If the other person then tossed off "your attitude needs some work," you'd blow up too — yet that's often exactly what we do only to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" is protecting
Telling a teacher "please change what you're doing" almost always hits a wall. The safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's responsible, just what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the child's safety, and the relief of catching a breath. The request must land on a concrete, doable change, like "can he sit on a ball just outside the circle?" If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding another arrangement that meets both sides.

16:07 A naptime conflict, cleanly taken apart
Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap; the teacher wanted her lying down, and she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state rules required offering a nap, and naptime was the teacher's own rest period. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll away, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and her rest, and Jen escaped the no-win cycle of calls home. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question
Compress all of the above into a single line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop" and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed — and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: The Thai Flood That Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter over quarter, Seagate's fell only 8%, and Seagate overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand redrew the hard drive rankings: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter over quarter, Seagate's fell only 8%, and Seagate overtook it to take the top spot.

What are the risks of geographic concentration in a manufacturing supply chain? This flood is a complete case study — industrial estate siting, zero inventory and a single point of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave the hard drive factories a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. For flood protection, developers installed ring levees up to two metres high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that precisely this kind of seemingly complete infrastructure created a false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what the manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focused on favouring farmers and rice corruption allegations. But the research does not support that blame. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data across the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster zone; reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame.

9:25 Why Seagate stalled even though it wasn't flooded
Seagate's factories in northern Korat were basically fine, but production stopped anyway — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and shut down directly after two of its plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain interlocks layer by layer: however safe the assembly line, if the motors don't come, the whole line stops. Seagate held its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by rapidly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 metres deep, and its quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose underlying supply chain could route around the break point faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 that it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced the acquisition of Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that fourth-quarter 2011 hard drive demand was about 180 million units, while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million; and the flood hit right in the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion short of expectations because of the hard drive shortage. A local flood, transmitted through zero inventory, became a global shortage just like that.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices didn't fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability only returned to pre-disaster levels about nine months later; retail prices fell back even more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the arithmetic with its own purchasing records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and returning to that level again had to wait until September 2013. Why is it easy to raise prices and hard to cut them? The author lists several readings: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought extra costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to fall permanently, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major manufacturers remained in the whole industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilise’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, it doubled down on defences. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometre flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-metre inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered several more rounds of major flooding, especially almost every year in the 2020s; in November of the most recent year it even rained in what was billed as a ‘once in 300 years’ event, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defences will be needed in future can only be tested by the next big flood.

item.title: AI designs viruses that infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media made it sound.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media made it sound.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and the biosecurity rhetoric, and also demonstrates how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural experiment
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy switch got the old vaccine, those after got the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — socioeconomic status, smoking, diet and other unmeasured factors could still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? Measure it with the E-value. This vaccine study's E-value is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong but is associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcome" could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 before a conclusion counts as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves concede that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation should not be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence data, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch that was then shown to be functional. If the media summarises this as "AI directly made a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The prompt given to the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across every genome the model generated. It works like a password saying "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve. This also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it lands on a functional pressure point.

56:55 AI swaps one gene and adds 58 mutations itself
EVO36's design idea was not to rewrite the whole thing but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans did the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated 58 additional mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that exist to re-adapt the foreign J protein to its local environment. Humans would not necessarily think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the power of single-point editing.

1:00:15 Mixed phages specifically target drug-resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already-resistant bacteria and cannot break through even after five passages; 16 AI-synthesised phages mixed together infected the originally resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should not bet on a single strain but should send in a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosecurity implications. Vincent pushed back on that wording directly on the show: the authors had already shown with reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what should be done is not to sound the alarm but to start building a safety framework. He also stressed that reconstructing a virus is not science fiction as long as you have enough sequence — precisely why frameworks are needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition but because they simply do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of faith" gets the policy response wrong — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but reaching them with information so they first know the vaccine exists.

item.title: Sports Betting Has Penetrated Gen Z, and the Regulatory Risk Is Underestimated
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
item.description: Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy; slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platforms as financial products, with future regulatory risk widely underestimated.
item.content:encoded:
Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy; slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platforms as financial products, with future regulatory risk widely underestimated.

A multi-angle look at the hidden dangers of financialised gambling, from wealth management and market structure to regulation, with forward-looking value for understanding how the younger generation invests and where policy may change.

3:06 Gen Z treats betting as a financial strategy
A Betterment survey shows 26% of Gen Z investors see sports betting as part of a long-term financial strategy; in a CNBC survey, 52% of Gen Z investors moved money out of investments and into sports betting over the past year. These numbers match Dave's experience with younger clients: betting has seeped into every layer of Gen Z, and wealth management has to confront it.

11:09 Slow losses are harder to recover from than a blowup
The insidious thing about sports betting is that dramatic blowups are rare; instead there is a steady drip of small losses, like betting hundreds of baseball games over a summer, slowly losing 10% a week, occasionally winning 20% and feeling good, round and round. That erosive financial despair is harder to recover from than one big mistake — it amounts to a chronic tax on numeracy.

17:14 Regulatory risk is widely underestimated
Dave argues most people ignore regulatory risk because they assume regulators respond to catastrophic events, when more likely some future administration or state regulator simply says "enough." He points to Florida and Texas banning speed cameras first, showing how unpredictable regulatory moves are. Companies depending on the current regulatory environment need to be wary.

21:14 Leveraged ETF products raise market-structure worries
In the same week, South Korea set strict investor-education thresholds for 2x leveraged products, Japan explicitly rejected single-stock leverage, while the US saw filings for 2x leveraged products that reset hourly. What worries Dave more is that the new ETFs try to hedge gambling risk using the futures market, but that futures market doesn't exist until the ETF has assets — the order is reversed, and it could divert resources from important financial participants whose job is to stabilise oil prices.

25:20 Big Tech earnings show financial gimmicks
Cameron notes Nvidia extended receivables to help customers, while hyperscaler customers extended payables to flatter free cash flow; Microsoft reclassified some capex into investing cash flow, lowering its capex guidance; activity inside SPVs doesn't show up on the statements. These "financial gimmicks" are common at cycle peaks — if the fundamentals were good, there'd be no need for them.

29:24 Less disclosure worsens information asymmetry
Cameron opposes moving earnings reports to semi-annual and cutting disclosure, arguing it worsens information asymmetry, benefits institutions with the resources to assemble information through the "mosaic effect," and reduces market efficiency. He also points out that regulatory trends like overturning the Chevron doctrine all concentrate power at the top, which is bad for innovation and competition.

38:27 The line between cultural appropriation and embrace
Cameron criticises Urban Outfitters for selling Nirvana tie-dye sweatpants to 12-year-olds, calling it a lack of respect for context, but Dave sees it as a possible gateway to the music: even a kid who starts out liking only the smiley face might end up listening to "Heart-Shaped Box." The argument reflects the tension between gatekeeping and openness in how culture spreads.

47:35 Finding role models as an adult means accepting imperfection
Dave shares a story about Keith Morris defusing a conflict at a Circle Jerks show, which sparks a discussion about role models. Cameron notes that as people age they learn to appreciate others' strengths while accepting their flaws, just as they do with their parents, taking the good and leaving the rest. Dave admits he can't find a living role model, because he knows no one is perfect.

item.title: Ion Drives: Push Slowly, and Win the Space Race Anyway
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.description: Rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. An ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny fraction of the propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.
item.content:encoded:
Rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. An ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny fraction of the propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.

This episode covers ion propulsion's principles, limits and applications in full — suited to anyone who wants a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion is now mainstream for deep space and satellites; those with no taste for engine minutiae can focus on the thrust and applications segments.

1:04 Ion propulsion wins on endurance
The rocket equation is cruel: to go faster you must throw away more mass, or throw it faster — but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, a tax collector's loop. Chemical rockets use high thrust to leave Earth quickly, but their exhaust velocity is capped by the energy stored in chemical bonds. Ion propulsion takes another route: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate a small number of charged particles to extremely high speeds and throw them out. The thrust is astonishingly small, yet it can persist for weeks, months, even years, ultimately accumulating a velocity change chemical rockets struggle to match.

4:04 Specific impulse and thrust are a trade-off
Specific impulse measures how efficiently propellant is used; chemical rockets manage only a few hundred seconds, while ion engines reach several thousand. But that efficiency rests on extremely low thrust: an ion engine can never lift off from the surface of Earth, the Moon or Mars — at most it can depart a small asteroid that an astronaut could jump off. It isn't physically impossible; it trades thrust for efficiency, and time for speed. A chemical rocket is a sprinter, an ion engine a marathon runner.

6:07 Two mainstream forms of electric propulsion
The classic gridded ion thruster ionises propellant atoms and accelerates them out through charged grids — high efficiency, but the grids are continuously eroded. Hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionise and accelerate propellant, with somewhat lower specific impulse but greater thrust and better suitability for satellites; they are the mainstay of modern electric propulsion. There are also micro electric jet systems for small satellites, and high-power plasma concepts — and the core difference among all of them ultimately comes down to how to get enough electrical power.

10:13 Why xenon is the default propellant
Propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same accelerating voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum — mass times velocity — so helium looks tempting. Yet at the same power, a higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium needs about 590 megajoules to ionise a kilogram, xenon only about 9 megajoules. Xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode the engine. It is today's high-end choice for ion propulsion, but costs about a thousand dollars per kilogram. Argon is far cheaper, and is the industrial choice of the future.

18:20 Slow rockets are the bedrock of space logistics
Ion propulsion is especially suited to missions already in orbit: spiralling orbits up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. Humans are impatient cargo, but supplies — water, metal, parts, propellant — don't care about being shipped slowly. Future Mars plans or lunar bases can use chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion to move people fast, while ion engines deliver the cargo slowly ahead of time. Machines do the dull work; the history of civilisation is written in freighters, ships, railways, trucks and containers.

26:25 Longevity is the core requirement, not a bonus
An ion thruster must run continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, power processing units must survive years of operation. A chemical engine burns for minutes, an ion engine for years — this isn't easier, it's a different direction in which things get hard. It also struggles to exploit the Oberth effect: a chemical rocket can burn hard and briefly at orbital perigee for a huge gain in orbital energy, while an ion engine's thrust is spread over months and loses that advantage for nothing.

30:26 Propellant isn't fuel, it's money
Propellant isn't just fuel; it is mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred and protected. Every kilogram of propellant saved is another kilogram available for instruments, shielding, cargo and lifetime. The key to the early space age was whether you could reach space; the key to the next era is whether you can move around in space cheaply. Ion propulsion isn't enough to put people on Mars, but it may be the key tool for building space infrastructure — exploration gets the headlines, logistics builds the civilisation.

31:26 A low-speed engine can build an interstellar civilisation
Today's ion engines cannot perform interstellar flight within a human lifetime, but far-future electric propulsion — with megavolt or even gigavolt accelerators, enormous power supplies and propellant measured in tonnes — would begin to approach an interstellar precursor vehicle. More importantly, even if ion engines never become interstellar drives, they remain key to building the infrastructure of an interstellar civilisation: before launching a starship you must first build collectors, mines, fuel depots, telescope arrays, habitats and shipyards. These must be moved, assembled, maintained and resupplied, and ion propulsion may be the best choice for that slow work. It isn't the starship engine itself; it is one of the engines that builds the civilisation, and then builds the starship.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Reach the Peak, but Choosing the Next Mountain Still Takes a Human
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.description: Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, picking the next mountain still depends on human intuition.
item.content:encoded:
Companies are being rebuilt as a series of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, picking the next mountain still depends on human intuition.

A structural judgment from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest opportunity in consumer AI is joy, not efficiency. The takes are often counterintuitive — useful for stress-testing your own product roadmap.

4:05 The AI era will not reproduce winner-take-all
The AI era will not play out the way mobile internet did, with winner-take-all dynamics: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, whereas every layer of the AI stack now has roughly 20 relevant participants. Two years ago everyone thought coding agents would end up with a single winner; today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable and Replit are all moving forward at once. Anish says the people at the frontier inside the labs believe what's actually happening is autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own processes — rather than recursive self-improvement, so there won't be a runaway winner that swallows everyone. The takeaway for founders: don't bet on a single full-stack giant; every layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term place.

10:08 CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
Employees probably don't need to worry too much about being replaced by AI — not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because CEO incentives are growth, not shrinkage. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion company. A Google executive friend told Anish the company isn't laying people off — it's using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the hard problem has become ‘what should we add to the roadmap’. When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving headcount to finding new things to do for a bigger goal.

15:12 Companies will become loops, and the next step needs a human to set it
The shape of a company is shifting from a list of roles and departments into a cascade of loops: first the automation of an individual's workflow, then functional loops, then loops that cross business units, and eventually loops running most of the company's operations. The loops themselves keep producing output, and that output becomes the input to the next layer of loops; some mechanism feeds the signal back to the CEO — when to adjust the business entity, when the strategy should change. This machinery can help a company climb to a local maximum, but after the plateau it must rely on human intuition to do out-of-distribution thinking and put the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Asking AI to directly come up with a million-dollar idea often fails, because humans can set the right direction while AI is only responsible for sweeping along a given slope.

32:24 Users want to spend time, not save it
Silicon Valley defaults to AI's value being efficiency; Anish thinks that's a misjudgment: most people don't actually want to save time, they want to spend it where it brings connection, love, progress and fun. The biggest products in history have always been entertainment and social, so AI's consumer opportunity is not ‘a few more minutes saved’ but building loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, and feel progress or fun. He criticizes the past 40 years of technology for extending intelligence while barely extending the soul; fitting AI into those desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

37:29 AI is decoupling skill from desire
Anish sees AI as not just a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface — it can split ‘skill’ and ‘desire’ apart. People who want to make music are no longer blocked by ‘I can't play piano’; people who want to write code don't have to first learn it to the point of being employable; personal identity is thereby amplified. He looks back at the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s, which greatly stimulated human potential, and argues today's world is in a low-risk state; AI has a chance to pull GDP growth from 2% to 10-15% — provided it raises not the speed of a single step but the scale of what a group dares to imagine.

1:04:42 Ideas that are too small now fail to raise money
Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was absurd; today, looking at deals at a16z, the standard has flipped — if an idea can still only be that small even with AI's help, they simply don't invest. ‘Unbounded ambition’ has become the core value for screening companies; Marc Andreessen's version is: we either go to the moon, or we leave a moon-sized crater.

1:09:48 Shipping something small every week is how you build product intuition
The most direct advice for product people is the old line: build more things. Find a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a ‘chassis’, run each new model through it, ship the finished thing, discuss it with people — that's the path to building AI intuition. The cadence only needs to be one small release a week; going crazy isn't sustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and the photo album, auto-scoring it, and finally generating 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but work like this lets you taste AI's ‘moments of joy’ over and over — once you've tasted it, you can't go back.

item.title: US Outposts Were Dangerous Bubbles: How the War on Terror Trapped Itself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.description: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became targets that drew in conflict. The harder they fought, the more bloated and immobile they got, until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
item.content:encoded:
US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became targets that drew in conflict. The harder they fought, the more bloated and immobile they got, until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.

Wesley Morgan served on the ground in Afghanistan and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success coexisting with strategic failure, worth pondering for anyone who cares about war and organizations.

5:00 The outpost became a dangerous bubble
In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan went into Afghanistan's Pech Valley with the troops and found that US outposts meant to provide security for villages had in fact become ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. Both the Americans and the enemy suffered few casualties; it was the villages outside the outposts that truly suffered. That contrast made him start asking: who built these outposts, why, and when — questions that ultimately produced his book The Hardest Place.

10:39 The US military grew heavier and dumber
From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006 the 10th Mountain Division could still reach remote areas by pickup truck and ATV, but by 2010, because of the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could barely get to those places and had to rely on special forces for offensive missions. This overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier reach.

12:51 Two ODA teams: restraint versus recklessness
In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an ‘inkblot’ approach, trying to build secure zones around district centers, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to get into the Korengal looking for a fight, and ended up entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as muscle for one faction, starting the Korengal ‘snowball’ that eventually became a fierce battlefield lasting years.

19:27 Three US tribes inside the military were incompatible
In eastern Afghanistan there were three ‘tribes’ within the US military: conventional forces; the Green Berets (working with local partners, such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police); and the joint special operations task force (such as Task Force 373, made up mainly of SEAL Team 6 and Rangers, conducting night raids). The three had different objectives and sometimes supported each other, but more often got in each other's way. For example, the task force might kill someone conventional forces could easily have arrested, while in remote areas conventional forces could not reach, only the task force could operate. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

24:56 Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
Many commanders lacked real understanding in counterinsurgency and could only rely on quantifiable performance metrics: ordnance dropped, miles of road built, number of meetings held. The book gives an example: 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, fought in Kunar Province for 15 months and lost 24 soldiers; its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent and 10,000 Beanie Babies handed out — metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

40:00 Navy admirals with ground-combat résumés
Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force generals and admirals have a chapter in their résumés utterly unlike the standard career path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces — submarine officers, nuclear engineers, naval aviators. For example, the current commander of Indo-Pacific Command, Sam Paparo, led the Nuristan PRT for a year. These assignments coincided with the fighting at Wana and Narisan, and they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. That experience became a unique mark on their careers.

43:18 Military-media relations went from transparent to hostile
Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which unit to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company- and platoon-level units. But today, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, military-media relations have deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of officers at battalion level and below sees the media as something terrifying. He argues the turning point was not the McChrystal affair but the second Obama term, when the military began restricting embeds and pushing the war out of sight, because the complicated message that ‘advisors’ were really ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

57:52 How Multicam became a badge of the elite
Morgan tells the story of how Multicam spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art-school graduate, lost the Army's camouflage competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special forces and became a badge of the elite. Crucially, the company Crye hinted to game producers that this was elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before it appeared in real photographs, building an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.

item.title: Kent State Shootings: Why the National Guard Opened Fire on Students
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-extracredits-肯特州立枪击-国民警卫队为何向学生开火/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-extracredits-肯特州立枪击-国民警卫队为何向学生开火/
item.description: In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on protesting students, killing 4. Confused orders, outdated tactics and an armed standoff turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.
item.content:encoded:
In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on protesting students, killing 4. Confused orders, outdated tactics and an armed standoff turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.

This episode reconstructs the full course of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the event, and directly helps in understanding the social fractures in America in the 1960s and 70s.

1:05 The National Guard enters campus under arms
On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen carrying M1 rifles, bayonets and tear gas entered Kent State University, stationed at the football field and guarding the ROTC building. This deployment enraged students; even those who had not been participating in the protests felt the war had come to their doorstep. But students were not especially afraid, because previously the Guard had usually only used tear gas or brawled when handling demonstrations, and had never shot and killed anyone. This time, however, unusually, the troops carried live ammunition.

3:08 Confused orders, and the governor pours fuel on the fire
Governor Rhodes's speech was full of inflammatory rhetoric, comparing the protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the KKK, calling them "the worst people in America." But in fact, his order to formally deploy the Guard did not come until May 5, while the troops had already arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government and the governor over the Guard's mission: the president believed the assembly had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban had not yet taken effect. This confused transmission of information laid the groundwork for the later conflict.

5:09 Rules changed on the fly, triggering a standoff
On the evening of May 3, students gathered in the plaza to protest, but local government abruptly moved the curfew from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as "changing the rules mid-game," and split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat down on the main road, blocking traffic and singing "Give Peace a Chance." Police and the Guard surrounded them, with helicopters circling overhead. In the end, the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to drive the students back to their dormitories, leaving at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

9:11 May 4: a peaceful assembly forms again
At 11 a.m. on May 4, about 2,000 students gathered in the plaza again. Although there was no official state of emergency, university officials still handed out leaflets saying the assembly was illegal. Guard commander General Canterbury insisted the demonstration was illegal, but students still spread word of the gathering through loudspeakers. By noon, the assembly was largely peaceful, with only some crude slogans. University police announced through loudspeakers that the assembly was illegal and demanded dispersal, but their voices were drowned out, and a few rocks flew at vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two rounds of tear gas, but they missed, and the wind blew the gas away instead.

12:13 13 seconds of fire, 67 bullets
The Guard advanced to clear the area, successfully dispersing most of the protesters, but one group of 52 pushed too far and was trapped in the fenced stadium, pelted with rocks. Ten minutes later, they received orders to withdraw and moved toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned around, raised their weapons, and fired a 13-second volley totaling 67 bullets. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away) and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Another 9 were wounded, the closest at 60 feet, the farthest at 750 feet.

14:16 One photograph changes America
After the shooting there was dead silence, and students stood frozen in place. 14-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio knelt beside Jeffrey Miller's body screaming, and 21-year-old photography student John Filo took the picture, which became an image that shocked the nation. But the conflict did not end; protests spread across the country, followed by the Hard Hat Riot, the Jackson State shootings and other events. The episode stresses that this history is strikingly similar to the present, and worth reflecting on.

item.title: She Spoke Up for Women's Rights and Was Executed for Treason
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-stuffmissed-她为女权呐喊-却被以叛国罪处死/

item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Olympe de Gouges is known for the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but she was killed not for her feminist arguments — she was killed for opposing the king's execution and attacking Robespierre.
item.content:encoded:
Olympe de Gouges is known for the Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but she was killed not for her feminist arguments — she was killed for opposing the king's execution and attacking Robespierre.

To understand women's political position and one individual's fate during the French Revolution. History buffs and people following women's-rights issues will be interested.

1:05 The Declaration of the Rights of Woman answers the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Olympe de Gouges is most famous for the 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she switched to the feminine form citoyenne — it looks completely different but sounds similar. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this one pamphlet, and her death sentence was not for calling for women's rights.

6:13 Biographical truth is mixed with novelistic invention
The first English biography of de Gouges, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, draws heavily on her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but the book is highly fictional. Its protagonist is widely considered a stand-in for herself, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. This parentage has never been confirmed.

14:19 The Comédie-Française crushed a woman playwright
Zamore et Mirza was written in 1784 and submitted anonymously; it was accepted the following year but its staging was repeatedly delayed. When de Gouges kept pressing, the theater revoked her right of entry and applied for her arrest. Between 1761 and 1789 the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only writer treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her position.

17:28 Slavery became the first abolitionist play
The play finally opened in 1789, but the setting moved from the East Indies to the Caribbean, the characters changed from Asians to Africans, and the title became Slavery of the Blacks. It is often considered France's first play to explicitly support abolition and to tell the story from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy men with colonial interests hired hecklers to disrupt it, and actors refused to blacken their skin for the roles.

23:32 The article rewrites all 17 articles one by one
The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted rights to citizens but excluded women, and the 1791 constitution restricted the vote to taxpaying men. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the 17-article format and rewrote each one. Where the original's Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, for instance, she added that a mother has the right to publicly declare her child's paternity. The whole document is dedicated to Marie Antoinette, urging her to advance women's rights.

28:39 Defending Louis XVI became the rope around her neck
Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed a constitutional monarchy suited France best, with the king as a symbol rather than a holder of power. At Louis XVI's treason trial in 1792 she volunteered to defend him, on the grounds that the monarchy had been abolished and a republic could not try a former king for acts committed while he reigned. Her logic was called strained; the king was executed anyway, and she was seen as a royalist.

30:43 Federalism got her arrested
In July 1793, de Gouges proposed that France's provinces govern themselves rather than form a unified republic, which was taken as a direct provocation. She underestimated the ferocious political atmosphere of the Terror, and voluntarily brought investigators to her office, thinking her work would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Saved was used as evidence against her for sympathizing with Marie Antoinette. She was ultimately executed for opposing the republican constitution.
